    - title: "E. Hairer and G. Wanner, Solving Ordinary Differential Equations II, Chapter VI: Iterative Methods—Nonlinear Equations"
      url: "https://www.unige.ch/~hairer/poly/chap6.pdf"
      locator: "§VI.3: exact-Jacobian Newton correction for a square nonlinear root"
    - title: "Tobin A. Driscoll and Richard J. Braun, Fundamentals of Numerical Computation, version 1.0"
      url: "https://fncbook.github.io/v1.0/nonlineqn/newtonsys.html"
      locator: "Chapter 4.5.2, equations (92)–(93): solve the Jacobian system for the Newton correction"
---

## Definition

Let $U,V$ be as in [[def-regular-minimum-energy-path-in-a-collision-free-tube]]. **Inputs:** an initial point $x_0\in U$, a unit initial mode reference $v_{\rm ref}\in\mathbb R^d$, a local-ball center $x_{\rm ref}\in U$, radius $r_{\rm loc}>0$, gradient tolerance $\tau_g\ge0$, eigenvalue margin $\gamma>0$, eigenpair residual tolerance $\tau_{\rm eig}\ge0$, mode-overlap threshold $0\le\tau_{\rm mode}<1$, and update budget $N\in\mathbb N_0$. Return the last point, aligned lowest-mode reference and one of `geometry-failure`, `outside-local-basin`, `gradient-residual-tolerance`, `budget-exhausted`, `eigensolve-tolerance-failure`, `index-one-branch-failure`, `mode-tracking-failure`, or a status returned by the vector Newton correction. At each iterate $x_k$, the eigensolver supplies an orthogonal matrix $Q=[q_1,\ldots,q_d]$, ordered approximate eigenvalues $\widehat\lambda_1\le\cdots\le\widehat\lambda_d$, and validated intervals $I_j=[\ell_j,u_j]$ in the sense of [[def-validated-eigenvalue-enclosures-for-an-index-one-hessian]]. Require every residual $\|H(x_k)q_j-\widehat\lambda_jq_j\|_2\le\tau_{\rm eig}$, $\sqrt d\,\tau_{\rm eig}\le\gamma/2$, and $\widehat\lambda_j\in I_j$. The Hessian $H=\nabla^2V$ is symmetric by [[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]].

For $k=0,\ldots,N$, in order:

1. If $x_k\notin U$, return `geometry-failure`. If $x_k\notin B_2(x_{\rm ref},r_{\rm loc})$, return `outside-local-basin`. Compute $g_k=\nabla V(x_k)$. If $\|g_k\|_2\le\tau_g$, return `gradient-residual-tolerance`; if $k=N$, return `budget-exhausted`.
2. If an eigenpair residual exceeds $\tau_{\rm eig}$, $\sqrt d\tau_{\rm eig}>\gamma/2$, or some $\widehat\lambda_j\notin I_j$, return `eigensolve-tolerance-failure`. If the validated intervals do not satisfy $u_1\le-\gamma$ and $\ell_j\ge\gamma$ for all $j\ge2$ (with the dimension-one convention in the definition), return `index-one-branch-failure`. If $|q_1^Tv_{\rm ref}|<\tau_{\rm mode}$, return `mode-tracking-failure`; otherwise replace $q_1$ by its sign-aligned representative with $q_1^Tv_{\rm ref}\ge0$ and use this as the next mode reference. This overlap check detects a mode-branch change but does not alter the Newton correction.
3. Call [[alg-newton-correction-for-vector-residuals]] with $A=H(x_k)$ and $r=g_k$. If its Jacobian is singular, return `singular-hessian`. Its correction $p_k$ is the exact Newton solution of $H(x_k)p_k=-g_k$ in the mathematical model; the eigenpair data certifies the index-one branch but does not replace this linear solve.
4. If $x_k+p_k\notin U$ or lies outside $B_2(x_{\rm ref},r_{\rm loc})$, return `outside-local-basin`. Otherwise set $x_{k+1}=x_k+p_k$ and continue.

An approximate eigensolve has a finite residual-tolerance branch and an explicit failure status. The definition makes no global-convergence claim. Local quadratic behavior is stated separately and requires the hypotheses of [[thm-updated-jacobian-newton-local-quadratic-convergence]].

## Statement

Let $L>0$, let $M\ge1$ be an integer, and let $R:[0,L]\to\mathbb R^d$ be a unit-speed $C^3$ curve with $M$ equal arc-length intervals of length $h=L/M$. Suppose $\|R''\|_2\le K_2$ and the coordinate third derivatives satisfy the bound in [[lem-centered-chord-and-unequal-step-tangent-error]] with constant $M_3$. For sufficiently small $h$, each chord length $\ell_i=\|R(ih)-R((i-1)h)\|_2$ satisfies $|\ell_i-h|\le C_1h^3$, where $C_1$ depends only on $K_2,M_3$. The piecewise-linear interpolant through the samples differs from $R$ in supremum norm by at most $C_2h^2$. If this polygon is redistributed by linear interpolation at equally spaced cumulative-length targets, the $j$th redistributed image is within $C_3h^2$ of $R(jh)$, for every $j=0,\ldots,M$.

Here $C^3$ on $[0,L]$ means that $R$ is the restriction of a $C^3$ curve on an open interval containing $[0,L]$; derivatives at the endpoints are the continuous one-sided values, and the unit-speed and derivative bounds are required on $[0,L]$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The unit-speed $C^3$ curve, equal arc-length mesh, derivative bounds, and small-mesh condition in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-regular-minimum-energy-path-in-a-collision-free-tube]]: arc-length parameterization has unit derivative.

[F2] [[lem-centered-chord-and-unequal-step-tangent-error]]: the coordinate third-derivative bound used here is $|R_j'''|\le M_3/\sqrt d$ on the path interval.

[F3] [[cor-taylor-lagrange-and-cauchy-remainders]]: its one-dimensional Lagrange formula applies to a scalar $C^3$ function on a closed interval when derivatives through order three are continuous to the endpoints; with degree two it bounds the remainder by $\sup|g'''|\,|u|^3/6$, and with degree one it bounds the remainder by $\sup|g''|\,|u|^2/2$.

[F4] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: differentiating a composition gives the derivative of the outer function applied to the derivative of the inner function.

[A1] The curve has the endpoint $C^3$ convention in the Statement, has unit speed on $[0,L]$, and has the stated bounds $\|R''\|_2\le K_2$ and coordinate third-derivative bound $M_3/\sqrt d$ on the whole interval; the interior $C^3$ convention is [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]].



**Given:** The data in the Statement.

## Proof

1.1 On each mesh interval $[s,s+h]$, apply the one-dimensional degree-two formula [F3] to each coordinate of the extended curve at $s$; the endpoint convention supplies the required derivative continuity, and [A1, F2] gives a remainder vector $r$ with $\|r\|_2\le M_3h^3/6$. Thus $R(s+h)-R(s)=hT+\frac{h^2}{2}K+r$ with $T=R'(s)$, $K=R''(s)$, and $\|K\|_2\le K_2$. Differentiating $\|R'(s)\|_2^2=1$ gives $T^TK=0$ by the chain rule [F4]. Hence $|\|R(s+h)-R(s)\|_2^2-h^2|\le C h^4$ for a constant depending only on $K_2,M_3$; for sufficiently small $h$ the chord is at least $h/2$, so division by its sum with $h$ yields $|\ell_i-h|\le C_1h^3$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, given, algebra]

1.2 For $s=ih+\theta h$ with $0\le\theta\le1$, apply the one-dimensional degree-one formula [F3] on $\lbrack ih,s\rbrack$ and $\lbrack ih,(i+1)h\rbrack$. The remainder bound in [F3] and $\|R''\|_2\le K_2$ give $R(s)=R(ih)+\theta hR'(ih)+O(K_2h^2)$ and $R((i+1)h)=R(ih)+hR'(ih)+O(K_2h^2)$. Subtracting the linear interpolant cancels the first-order term, so the pointwise interpolation error is bounded by $C_2h^2$, uniformly over all intervals. [A1, F1, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 Let $p_i=\sum_{m=1}^{i}\ell_m$ and $L_h=p_M$. Step 1.1 gives $|p_i-ih|\le iC_1h^3\le C_1Lh^2$ and $|L_h-L|\le C_1Lh^2$. Thus the redistributed target $q_j=jL_h/M$ satisfies $|q_j-jh|\le C_1Lh^2$. Each segment has length at least $h/2$ for small $h$. If target $q_j$ lies on segment $i$ at fraction $\theta$, then $p_{i-1}+\theta\ell_i=q_j$; combining $|p_{i-1}-(i-1)h|\le C_1Lh^2$, $|q_j-jh|\le C_1Lh^2$, and $|\ell_i-h|\le C_1h^3$ gives $|(i-1)h+\theta h-jh|\le C h^2$. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The point on the true curve at parameter $(i-1)h+\theta h$ is within $C_2h^2$ of the redistributed polygon point by step 1.2, and it is within $C h^2$ of $R(jh)$ by unit speed and step 2.1. The triangle inequality gives the claimed $C_3h^2$ bound, including endpoints where redistribution fixes the endpoints. [F1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $d\ge2$, let $V\in C^4(U,\mathbb R)$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, and let $x\in U$. Put $H=\nabla^2V(x)$ and $\epsilon_g=\|\nabla V(x)\|_2$. Suppose a validated ordered eigenvalue enclosure certifies index one with gap $\gamma>0$ in the sense of [[def-validated-eigenvalue-enclosures-for-an-index-one-hessian]]. If $\epsilon_g=0$, then $x$ is an exact critical point with Hessian index one.

If $\epsilon_g>0$, put $\rho=2\epsilon_g/\gamma$. Assume $B_2(x,2\rho)\subset U$, the Hessian is $L$-Lipschitz there, and $L\rho/\gamma\le1/2$. Then there is exactly one critical point $x_*$ in $\overline B_2(x,\rho)$, it satisfies $\|x_*-x\|_2\le\rho$, and its Hessian has exactly one negative eigenvalue and no zero eigenvalues. The reported residual $\epsilon_g$, gap $\gamma$, conditioning bound $1/\gamma$, Hessian Lipschitz constant $L$, and radius condition are part of the certificate; a residual or a Ritz value alone is not a certificate.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The potential, point, gradient residual, interval evidence, gap, and local Hessian-Lipschitz hypotheses in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-validated-eigenvalue-enclosures-for-an-index-one-hessian]]: the validated intervals certify $\lambda_1(H)\le-\gamma$ and $\lambda_j(H)\ge\gamma$ for $j\ge2$.

[F2] Since $V\in C^4$, it is $C^2$, and [[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]] gives $H^T=H$. In the standard Euclidean inner product this is a self-adjoint endomorphism, so [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]] gives an orthonormal eigenbasis.

[F3] [[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]] and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] define $H$ and the gradient. [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] identifies the matrix of $D(\nabla V)$ with the gradient Jacobian; [[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]] makes its entries agree with the Hessian convention. A critical point is a zero of the gradient.

[F4] [[lem-local-root-from-uniformly-small-residual]]: if $DF(x)$ is invertible, has inverse norm at most $\beta$, and is $L$-Lipschitz on a sufficiently large ball, then $\|F(x)\|$ small enough gives a unique nearby zero within $2\beta\|F(x)\|$.

[F5] [[thm-courant-fischer-min-max-principle]]: the largest eigenvalue is the maximum Rayleigh quotient, and the second largest is at most the maximum Rayleigh quotient on the orthogonal complement of a leading eigenvector.



**Given:** The data in the Statement.

## Proof

1.1 By [F1], the eigenvalues of $H$ are all at least distance $\gamma$ from zero. Using the orthonormal eigenbasis in [F2], $H$ is invertible and $\|H^{-1}\|_{\rm op}\le1/\gamma$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 If $\epsilon_g=0$, [F3] says $x$ is critical, and [F1] says its Hessian has exactly one negative eigenvalue. Suppose henceforth $\epsilon_g>0$ and use the inverse bound $\beta=1/\gamma$ from step 1.1. The radius in [F4] is then exactly $2\beta\epsilon_g=\rho$, and its Lipschitz condition is $\beta L\rho=L\rho/\gamma\le1/2$. Since $B_2(x,2\rho)\subset U$, every hypothesis of [F4] holds on the stated ball, so there is exactly one zero $x_*$ of $\nabla V$ in $\overline B_2(x,\rho)$ and $\|x_*-x\|_2\le\rho$. [F1, F3, F4, given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Set $A=-H(x)$ and $E=-(H(x_*)-H(x))$. Then $A$ is symmetric with largest eigenvalue at least $\gamma$ and second-largest at most $-\gamma$. The Lipschitz hypothesis and $\|x_*-x\|_2\le\rho$ from step 2.1 give $\|E\|_{\rm op}\le L\rho\le\gamma/2$. [F1, F2, step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 Let $q_1$ be a unit leading eigenvector of $A$. The maximum Rayleigh formula in [F5] yields $\lambda_1(A+E)\ge q_1^T(A+E)q_1\ge\lambda_1(A)-\|E\|_{\rm op}\ge\gamma/2>0$. The second-eigenvalue min-max formula in [F5], applied to $q_1^\perp$, yields $\lambda_2(A+E)\le\lambda_2(A)+\|E\|_{\rm op}\le-\gamma/2<0$. Every later eigenvalue is at most the second, so $A+E=-H(x_*)$ has exactly one positive eigenvalue and no zero eigenvalue. Thus $H(x_*)$ has exactly one negative eigenvalue and no zero eigenvalues. Together with step 2.1 this proves the stated local certificate; if $\epsilon_g=0$, step 2.1 already proved it. [F1, F2, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $L>0$, let $M\ge2$ be an integer, and let $R$ be a regular MEP as in [[def-regular-minimum-energy-path-in-a-collision-free-tube]], now parameterized by arc length on $[0,L]$, with $R\in C^3$ under the endpoint convention of [[lem-arc-length-polyline-interpolation-error]] and the bounds of [[lem-centered-chord-and-unequal-step-tangent-error]] and [[lem-arc-length-polyline-interpolation-error]]. Let $R_i=R(ih)$ for $i=0,\ldots,M$, $Mh=L$, and assume every interior centered chord is nonzero. Suppose $\|\nabla V(R(s))\|_2\le G$ along the curve and $0<h\le1$. Use the centered unit tangent $\widehat t_i=(R_{i+1}-R_{i-1})/\|R_{i+1}-R_{i-1}\|_2$. Then the projected string force at each interior sample satisfies

$$\|(I-\widehat t_i\widehat t_i^T)\nabla V(R_i)\|_2\le C_Fh^2.$$

If the equal-spacing spring residual $k(\ell_i^+-\ell_i^-)\widehat t_i$ is also evaluated on these samples, then its norm is at most $C_Sh^3$ for fixed $k$. Equal-length polyline redistribution of the exact samples changes each image by at most $C_Rh^2$. The constants depend on the stated derivative bounds, $G$, $k$, and the path, not on $M$. The projected-force conclusion is for the centered-tangent string residual; it does not assert second-order consistency for the improved energy-selected NEB tangent.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The $C^3$ unit-speed regular MEP, mesh, derivative bounds, and gradient bound in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-regular-minimum-energy-path-in-a-collision-free-tube]]: $P_{t(s)}^\perp\nabla V(R(s))=0$ and $t(s)=R'(s)$ for the unit-speed parameterization.

[F2] [[lem-centered-chord-and-unequal-step-tangent-error]]: the open-interval $C^3$ extension and bounded third derivatives give $\|\widehat t_i-t(ih)\|_2\le C_th^2$ for the centered chord under the stated regularity and nondegeneracy.

[F3] [[lem-arc-length-polyline-interpolation-error]]: under its endpoint $C^3$ convention, sampled chord lengths satisfy $|\ell_i-h|\le C_1h^3$, and equal-length interpolation has image error at most $C_Rh^2$.

[F4] [[alg-finite-image-string-method]]: the string residual uses the normal projection formed from the centered chord, with endpoints fixed and linear equal-length redistribution.



**Given:** The data and conventions in the Statement.

## Proof

1.1 For unit vectors $u,v$, $uu^T-vv^T=(u-v)u^T+v(u-v)^T$, so $\|uu^T-vv^T\|_{\rm op}\le2\|u-v\|_2$. Apply this with $u=\widehat t_i$ and $v=t(ih)$. Since $P_v^\perp\nabla V(R_i)=0$ by [F1], we obtain $\|P_{\widehat t_i}^\perp\nabla V(R_i)\|_2\le2G\|\widehat t_i-t(ih)\|_2\le2GC_th^2$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

1.2 By [F3], write each neighboring chord length as $\ell_i^\pm=h+e_i^\pm$ with $|e_i^\pm|\le C_1h^3$. Hence $k|\ell_i^+-\ell_i^-|\le2kC_1h^3$, because the triangle inequality bounds the difference by $|e_i^+|+|e_i^-|$. [F3, given, algebra]

2.1 The spring term is tangent and has the bound in step 1.2; the normal component has the bound in step 1.1. Since $h\le1$, $h^3\le h^2$, so their sum is bounded by $(2GC_t+2kC_1)h^2$. The string redistribution error is the last assertion of [F3]. These statements concern the centered-tangent string discretization specified by [F4]; the improved NEB tangent is a different branch and is treated separately. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $V\in C^4(U,\mathbb R)$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, and put $F=\nabla V$. At any accepted update of [[alg-index-one-eigenvector-following-step]], the step is the unique vector $p$ solving

$$DF(x)p=-F(x),\qquad DF(x)=\nabla^2V(x).$$

Suppose $x_*$ is a critical point, its Hessian is nonsingular with exactly one negative eigenvalue, and the Hessian is Lipschitz on a neighborhood of $x_*$. Then for all initial points in a sufficiently small ball about $x_*$, every update that the algorithm attempts before it stops is the ordinary exact-Jacobian Newton update and satisfies the local quadratic estimate supplied by [[thm-updated-jacobian-newton-local-quadratic-convergence]]. A gradient or eigensolve stopping status creates no later update, and no global-start guarantee is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The smooth potential, square gradient residual, accepted branch checks, nonsingular index-one critical point, and local Hessian-Lipschitz hypothesis in the Statement.

[F1] [[alg-index-one-eigenvector-following-step]]: after its eigenpair and enclosure checks, it calls the square vector Newton correction with Jacobian $H(x)=\nabla^2V(x)$ and residual $\nabla V(x)$.

[F2] [[alg-newton-correction-for-vector-residuals]]: if the Jacobian is invertible, its correction is the unique $p$ solving $J(x)p=-F(x)$.

[F3] [[thm-updated-jacobian-newton-local-quadratic-convergence]]: for a $C^2$ square residual with a simple zero and locally Lipschitz Jacobian that is invertible at the zero, exact-Jacobian Newton updates from a sufficiently small ball remain local and satisfy a quadratic error bound; the finite method may stop first.

[F4] [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and [[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]] fix the Jacobian, gradient, and Hessian conventions. [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] identifies the matrix of $D(\nabla V)$ with the gradient Jacobian, and [[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]] makes its entries agree with $\nabla^2V$. Critical points are precisely zeros of $F$.

[A1] The Hessian at an index-one critical point is nonsingular: its one negative eigenvalue and all remaining positive eigenvalues are nonzero.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses of the Statement.

1.1 At an accepted update, [F1] supplies the exact Hessian Jacobian and gradient residual to the Newton-correction procedure, and its validated ordered enclosures put every Hessian eigenvalue at distance at least $\gamma$ from zero. Thus the Hessian is invertible; [F2] makes the returned correction the unique solution of $\nabla^2V(x)p=-\nabla V(x)$, so the selected step is exactly the vector Newton step. [F1, F2, F4]

1.2 Let $x_*$ be the critical point. By [F4], $F(x_*)=0$ and $DF(x_*)=\nabla^2V(x_*)$ is invertible by [A1]. Since $V\in C^4$, $F$ is $C^2$; the assumed local Hessian-Lipschitz bound is a local Lipschitz bound on $DF$. Thus the hypotheses of [F3] hold. [A1, F3, F4, given]

2.1 The algorithm's update, whenever it is attempted, is the exact correction from step 1.1. Applying [F3] to this recurrence gives the asserted local quadratic bound and invariant neighborhood for every attempted update; if the algorithm stops on a residual or certification branch, there is no later point to which that update claim applies. No conclusion outside the local hypotheses follows. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

Let $d\ge2$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $V\in C^4(U,\mathbb R)$ using the convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Fix $x\in U$. Put $H=\nabla^2V(x)$ and suppose a validated ordered eigenvalue enclosure certifies index one with gap $\gamma>0$ as in [[def-validated-eigenvalue-enclosures-for-an-index-one-hessian]], so $\lambda_1(H)\le-\gamma$ and $\lambda_j(H)\ge\gamma$ for $j\ge2$. Let $v$ be a unit direction accepted by the rotation test of [[alg-finite-budget-dimer-mode-following]], with paired-force estimate $D_\epsilon$ and $\|(I-vv^T)D_\epsilon\|_2\le\tau_{\rm rot}$. Suppose each force evaluation has Euclidean error at most $\eta$, the third derivatives of each gradient coordinate are bounded by $M_4$ on the dimer segments, and set

$$\delta:=\frac{\sqrt d\,M_4}{6}\epsilon^2+\frac{\eta}{\epsilon}.$$

If $\delta\le\gamma/4$ and the measured Rayleigh estimate $v^TD_\epsilon\le-\gamma/2$, then the sine of the angle from $v$ to the lowest-eigenvalue line of $H$ satisfies

$$\sin\angle(v,q_1):=\sqrt{1-|q_1^Tv|^2}\le\frac{4(\tau_{\rm rot}+\delta)}{5\gamma},$$

where $q_1$ is any unit eigenvector for $\lambda_1(H)$. This is a conditional mode bound; rotation success alone is not an index certificate.

Let $\epsilon_g=\|\nabla V(x)\|_2$. If $\epsilon_g=0$, $x$ itself is an index-one critical point. If $\epsilon_g>0$, put $\rho=2\epsilon_g/\gamma$ and additionally assume $B_2(x,2\rho)\subset U$, $H(\cdot)=\nabla^2V(\cdot)$ is $L$-Lipschitz on that ball, and $L\rho/\gamma\le1/2$. Then there is a unique index-one critical point $x_*$ in $\overline B_2(x,\rho)$ and

$$\|x_*-x\|_2\le\rho=\frac{2\epsilon_g}{\gamma}.$$

The dimer direction bound does not replace the validated eigenvalue enclosure or the residual, inverse, and Hessian-Lipschitz conditions in this local saddle certificate.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The potential and point, validated ordered eigenvalue enclosure, accepted unit dimer direction, paired-force estimate and error data, gradient residual, and (when $\epsilon_g>0$) the local Hessian-Lipschitz hypotheses in the Statement.

[A1] The validated intervals establish $\lambda_1(H)\le-\gamma$ and $\lambda_j(H)\ge\gamma$ for $j\ge2$ ([[def-validated-eigenvalue-enclosures-for-an-index-one-hessian]]).

[A2] The dimer rotation test has accepted $v$ with $\|(I-vv^T)D_\epsilon\|_2\le\tau_{\rm rot}$, and $v^TD_\epsilon\le-\gamma/2$.

[A3] The force errors and third-derivative bound give the stated value $\delta$.

[A4] For the local saddle conclusion with $\epsilon_g>0$, the stated ball, Hessian-Lipschitz, and radius hypotheses hold.

[F1] Since $V\in C^4$, it is $C^2$; [[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]] makes $H$ symmetric, hence self-adjoint in the standard Euclidean inner product, so [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]] gives an orthonormal eigenbasis.

[F2] [[lem-dimer-central-force-hessian-vector-error]]: $\|D_\epsilon-Hv\|_2\le\delta$ under the stated paired-force and derivative-error bounds.

[F3] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: for a unit vector $v$, $|v^Tw|\le\|w\|_2$; orthogonal projection $I-vv^T$ does not increase Euclidean norm, by the orthogonal decomposition into parallel and perpendicular parts.

[F4] [[thm-local-index-one-saddle-certificate-from-enclosures]]: the eigenvalue gap, gradient residual, inverse bound, and local Hessian-Lipschitz/radius conditions give the stated unique nearby index-one critical point.



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [F1], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis $q_1,\ldots,q_d$ for $H$, ordered so that their eigenvalues are $\lambda_1\le\cdots\le\lambda_d$. Since $v$ is unit, write $v=\sum_{j=1}^d c_jq_j$ with $\sum_jc_j^2=1$. [A1, F1, given]

2.1 Put $\mu=v^THv$. From [F2] and [F3], $|v^T(D_\epsilon-Hv)|\le\delta$, so $\mu\le v^TD_\epsilon+\delta\le-\gamma/2+\gamma/4=-\gamma/4$. [A2, A3, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Since $v^THv=\mu$, $(I-vv^T)Hv=(H-\mu I)v$. By [A2], [F2], and the projection bound in [F3], $\|(H-\mu I)v\|_2\le\|(I-vv^T)D_\epsilon\|_2+\|(I-vv^T)(Hv-D_\epsilon)\|_2\le\tau_{\rm rot}+\delta$. [A2, A3, F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For every $j\ge2$, [A1] and step 2.1 give $\lambda_j-\mu\ge\gamma+\gamma/4=5\gamma/4$. Expanding step 3.1 in the eigenbasis from step 1.1 yields $\left(\frac{5\gamma}{4}\right)^2\sum_{j=2}^dc_j^2\le\sum_{j=2}^d(\lambda_j-\mu)^2c_j^2\le\|(H-\mu I)v\|_2^2\le(\tau_{\rm rot}+\delta)^2$. As $\sum_{j=2}^dc_j^2=1-|q_1^Tv|^2$, taking nonnegative square roots proves the stated sine-angle bound. [A1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 If $\epsilon_g=0$, the zero-residual branch of [[thm-local-index-one-saddle-certificate-from-enclosures]] and [A1] make $x$ an exact index-one critical point. If $\epsilon_g>0$, [A1] and [A4] are exactly the enclosure, residual, and neighborhood hypotheses of [F4]; applying it gives the unique index-one critical point in the radius-$\rho$ ball and the bound $\|x_*-x\|_2\le2\epsilon_g/\gamma$. This local error conclusion is independent of the mode-angle estimate and adds no global convergence claim for the finite dimer iteration. [A1, A4, F4, step 4.1, given] ∎

## Statement

There is a $C^\infty$ potential on a collision-free annular sector and a regular MEP with strictly monotone energy on an interior arc such that the improved NEB monotone branch has projected-force error $\Theta(h)$ on equal-arc samples. In particular, the improved-tangent NEB force in [[alg-improved-tangent-climbing-neb]] has no general $O(h^2)$ projected-force consistency bound, even when the curve and potential are smooth and the chord is nondegenerate.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The improved tangent rule in [[alg-improved-tangent-climbing-neb]], the normal-projection MEP condition in [[def-regular-minimum-energy-path-in-a-collision-free-tube]], and the limit supplier below.

[F1] [[alg-improved-tangent-climbing-neb]]: on a strictly increasing-energy triple, the selected unnormalized tangent is $\Delta_i^+=R_{i+1}-R_i$.

[F2] [[def-regular-minimum-energy-path-in-a-collision-free-tube]]: a regular MEP has zero gradient component normal to its true unit tangent.

[F3] [[cor-sin-x-over-x-limit]]: $\lim_{u\to0}\sin(u)/u=1$.

[F4] [[prop-central-string-projected-force-consistency]]: the proved $O(h^2)$ projected-force estimate is for the centered-tangent string discretization.

[A1] In this chart $\partial_sX=((R_0+n)/R_0)T(s)$ and $\partial_nX=N(s)$, with $T(s)=(-\sin(s/R_0),\cos(s/R_0))$ and $N(s)=(\cos(s/R_0),\sin(s/R_0))$.



**Given:** A radius $R_0>0$, an arc-length coordinate $s$ in $(-R_0\pi/4,R_0\pi/4)$, and a normal coordinate $n\in(-R_0/4,R_0/4)$. Define $X(s,n)=(R_0+n)(\cos(s/R_0),\sin(s/R_0))$. This is a smooth injective coordinate chart because $R_0+n>0$ and the angle interval has length less than $2\pi$. Put $a=R_0\pi/6$, $W(s)=(s^2-a^2)^2$, and $V(X(s,n))=W(s)+\tfrac12n^2$ on the chart. The curve $R(s)=X(s,0)$ is regular and unit speed.

## Proof

1.1 At $n=0$, [A1] gives $\partial_sX=T(s)$ and $\partial_nX=N(s)$, an orthonormal coordinate basis. The potential has coordinate derivatives $\partial_sV=W'(s)$ and $\partial_nV=n=0$, so $\nabla V(R(s))=W'(s)T(s)$. Therefore its component normal to $T(s)$ vanishes and $R$ is a regular MEP by [F2]. [A1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 We have $W'(s)=4s(s^2-a^2)>0$ for $-a<s<0$ and $W'(s)<0$ for $0<s<a$, so the energy is strictly increasing then decreasing. Since $V=W(s)+n^2/2\ge0$ with equality exactly at $(s,n)=(\pm a,0)$, those two endpoints are global minima on the sector. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 On an equal-arc mesh of width $h$ in the increasing subarc $(-a,0)$, [F1] selects the forward chord. For a circle, $R(s+h)-R(s)$ points in direction $T(s+h/2)$, so the angle between its normalized direction and $T(s)$ is exactly $h/(2R_0)$. The true gradient magnitude there is $|W'(s)|$, and its projection onto the normal complement of $T(s+h/2)$ has norm $|W'(s)|\sin(h/(2R_0))$. [A1, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Fix $s$ strictly inside the subarc, so $|W'(s)|>0$. By [F3], the ratio of this force error to $h$ tends to $|W'(s)|/(2R_0)>0$ as $h\to0$. The chord length is $2R_0\sin(h/(2R_0))>0$ for small $h$, so there is no tangent degeneracy. A quantity whose ratio to $h$ tends to a positive number cannot be $O(h^2)$; this proves the claim and, by [F4], distinguishes this one-sided estimate from the centered-string estimate. [F3, F4, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $d\ge2$, let $V\in C^4(U,\mathbb R)$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ using the convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], and let $x_*$ be a critical point with Hessian $H_*:=\nabla^2V(x_*)$ ordered as $\lambda_1(H_*)\le\cdots\le\lambda_d(H_*)$. Suppose

$$\lambda_1(H_*)\le-2\gamma,\qquad \lambda_j(H_*)\ge2\gamma\ (j\ge2),\qquad \|H_*\|_{\rm op}\le\Lambda$$

for $\gamma>0$ and $\Lambda\ge2\gamma$. Let the closed ball $\overline B_2(x_*,r)$ lie in $U$, let the Hessian be $L$-Lipschitz there, and assume $Lr\le\gamma$. At every iterate $x$ in this ball, suppose a validated Hessian enclosure gives $\lambda_1(H(x))\le-\gamma$ and $\lambda_j(H(x))\ge\gamma$ for $j\ge2$, and accepted dimer data satisfy the hypotheses of [[thm-dimer-mode-perturbation-and-local-saddle-error]] with uniform rotation residual $\tau_{\rm rot}$ and HVP error bound $\delta\le\gamma/4$. Define

$$\alpha:=\frac{4(\tau_{\rm rot}+\delta)}{5\gamma},\qquad q:=\max\left\{|1+\sigma\lambda_1(H_*)|,\ \max_{2\le j\le d}|1-\sigma\lambda_j(H_*)|\right\},$$

where $0<\sigma<2/\Lambda$. Suppose the finite dimer saddle translation of [[alg-finite-budget-dimer-mode-following]] uses a unit direction $v$ from those accepted data and a computed gradient $\widehat g(x)$ with $\|\widehat g(x)-\nabla V(x)\|_2\le\eta$. Put

$$\kappa:=q+\frac{\sigma Lr}{2}+2\sigma\left(\alpha+\frac{Lr}{3\gamma}\right)\left(\Lambda+\frac{Lr}{2}\right).$$

If $\kappa<1$ and $\sigma\eta\le(1-\kappa)r$, then every attempted translation starting at $\|x_0-x_*\|_2\le r$ remains in the ball and obeys

$$\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|_2\le\kappa\|x_k-x_*\|_2+\sigma\eta,$$

and consequently

$$\|x_k-x_*\|_2\le\kappa^k\|x_0-x_*\|_2+\frac{\sigma\eta(1-\kappa^k)}{1-\kappa}.$$

Thus exact translation gradients give local contraction, while a fixed bounded translation-force error gives the stated finite noise floor. The conclusion is conditional on a validated gap and accepted dimer mode at every attempted iterate; a finite rotation cap or missing spectral enclosure gives no such guarantee.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The critical point, Hessian gap and norm bound, Hessian-Lipschitz ball, validated enclosures, accepted dimer data, translation step size, and gradient-evaluation error bound in the Statement.

[A1] At $x_*$, $\lambda_1(H_*)\le-2\gamma$, all other eigenvalues are at least $2\gamma$, and $\|H_*\|_{\rm op}\le\Lambda$.

[A2] On $B_2(x_*,r)$, the Hessian is $L$-Lipschitz, $Lr\le\gamma$, and each attempted point has the stated validated index-one enclosure.

[A3] At each attempted point the accepted dimer data have $\|(I-vv^T)D_\epsilon\|_2\le\tau_{\rm rot}$, $v^TD_\epsilon\le-\gamma/2$, and HVP error at most $\delta\le\gamma/4$.

[A4] Each translation uses step $\sigma$ and a computed gradient with error at most $\eta$; $\kappa<1$ and $\sigma\eta\le(1-\kappa)r$.

[F1] [[thm-dimer-mode-perturbation-and-local-saddle-error]]: the accepted dimer data in [A3] give $\sin\angle(v,q_x)\le\alpha$ for a unit lowest-eigenvalue eigenvector $q_x$ of $H(x)$.

[F2] [[thm-local-leading-eigenvector-stability-under-eigengap]]: for a symmetric matrix with leading eigenvalue gap $g$ and symmetric perturbation norm $\epsilon<g/2$, the leading eigenvalue remains simple and the sine of its eigenvector-line angle is at most $\epsilon/(g-\epsilon)$.

[F3] [[lem-vector-newton-correction-error-under-lipschitz-jacobian]]: if $\nabla V(x_*)=0$ and the Hessian is $L$-Lipschitz on a convex ball, then $\|\nabla V(x)-H_*(x-x_*)\|_2\le(L/2)\|x-x_*\|_2^2$.

[F4] [[alg-finite-budget-dimer-mode-following]]: the saddle translation is $x^+=x+\sigma[-\widehat g+2(\widehat g^Tv)v]$ when the finite rotation and force branches permit an update.

[F5] [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], [[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]], and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] fix the derivative conventions. [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] identifies the matrix of $D(\nabla V)$ with the gradient Jacobian; [[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]] makes those entries agree with $H=\nabla^2V$. [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]] supplies the induced Euclidean operator norm.

[F6] Since $V\in C^4$, it is $C^2$, and [[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]] makes each Hessian in the proof symmetric. The standard Euclidean inner product then makes the corresponding endomorphism self-adjoint, so [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]] gives an orthonormal eigenbasis.



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct perturbation and error recurrence.

1.1 By [F6], choose a unit eigenvector $q_*$ for $\lambda_1(H_*)$. The leading eigenvalue of $-H_*$ is $-\lambda_1(H_*)$, and its gap from the second eigenvalue is $g_*:=\lambda_2(H_*)-\lambda_1(H_*)\ge4\gamma$. For $e=x-x_*$, the perturbation $E=-(H(x)-H_*)$ is symmetric and satisfies $\|E\|_{\rm op}\le L\|e\|_2\le Lr\le\gamma<g_*/2$. Applying [F2] to $-H_*$ and $-H(x)$ shows their leading eigenvector lines differ by sine at most $Lr/(4\gamma-Lr)\le Lr/(3\gamma)$. The leading eigenvector of $-H(x)$ is a lowest eigenvector $q_x$ of $H(x)$. [A1, A2, F2, F5, F6, given, algebra]

1.2 Set $P_*=q_*q_*^T$ and $A_*=-I+2P_*$. This is an orthogonal reflection, so $\|A_*\|_{\rm op}=1$. In an orthonormal eigenbasis of $H_*$ supplied by [F6], $I+\sigma A_*H_*$ has eigenvalues $1+\sigma\lambda_1(H_*)$ on $q_*$ and $1-\sigma\lambda_j(H_*)$ on its orthogonal complement; hence its operator norm is $q$. Because every $|\lambda_j(H_*)|\in[2\gamma,\Lambda]$ and $0<\sigma<2/\Lambda$, each displayed factor has absolute value strictly less than one, so $q<1$. [A1, F2, F5, F6, given, algebra]

2.1 For unit vectors $u,w$, the rank-one orthogonal projections satisfy $\|uu^T-ww^T\|_{\rm op}=\sin\angle(u,w)$. To see this, choose the sign of $w$ so $u^Tw\ge0$, write $w=(\cos\theta)u+(\sin\theta)z$ with $z\perp u$ unit, and represent $uu^T-ww^T$ on $\operatorname{span}\{u,z\}$; its $2\times2$ matrix has eigenvalues $\pm\sin\theta$, while it vanishes on the orthogonal complement. Applying the operator-norm triangle inequality through $q_x$ and using [F1] and step 1.1 gives $\|vv^T-q_*q_*^T\|_{\rm op}\le\alpha+Lr/(3\gamma)$. [A2, A3, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 By [F3], $\nabla V(x)=H_*e+r_x$ with $\|r_x\|_2\le(L/2)\|e\|_2^2$. Therefore the exact-mode translation satisfies $\|x+\sigma A_*\nabla V(x)-x_*\|_2\le q\|e\|_2+\frac{\sigma L}{2}\|e\|_2^2\le\left(q+\frac{\sigma Lr}{2}\right)\|e\|_2$. Also $\|\nabla V(x)\|_2\le(\Lambda+Lr/2)\|e\|_2$. [A1, A2, F3, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 For the accepted dimer direction set $A_v=-I+2vv^T$. It is also an orthogonal reflection. By [F4], the actual update is $x^+=x+\sigma A_v\widehat g(x)$. Thus $\|A_v\widehat g-A_*\nabla V(x)\|_2\le\|A_v-A_*\|_{\rm op}\|\nabla V(x)\|_2+\eta$, and $\|A_v-A_*\|_{\rm op}=2\|vv^T-q_*q_*^T\|_{\rm op}\le2(\alpha+Lr/(3\gamma))$ by step 2.1. Combining with step 2.2 proves $\|x^+-x_*\|_2\le\kappa\|e\|_2+\sigma\eta$. [A2, A4, F4, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 If $\|e\|_2\le r$, step 3.1 and [A4] give $\|x^+-x_*\|_2\le\kappa r+\sigma\eta\le r$, so each attempted update stays in the ball and the recurrence can be iterated. Induction on $k$ yields $\|x_k-x_*\|_2\le\kappa^k\|x_0-x_*\|_2+\sigma\eta\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\kappa^j$. Since $0\le\kappa<1$, the finite geometric sum is $(1-\kappa^k)/(1-\kappa)$, giving the stated error bound. [A4, step 3.1, induction, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $L>0$ and let $M\ge2$ be an integer. Let $V$ and $U$ satisfy [[def-regular-minimum-energy-path-in-a-collision-free-tube]], and let $R_*:[0,L]\to U$ be a $C^3$ unit-speed regular MEP with fixed endpoints, using the endpoint extension convention of [[lem-arc-length-polyline-interpolation-error]]. For $h=L/M$, let $z_h=(R_*(h),\ldots,R_*((M-1)h))$ be its interior samples and let $I_h$ be piecewise-linear reconstruction with the same fixed endpoints.

In a local coordinate chart, choose a smooth orthonormal normal frame $Q_i$ at each centered discrete tangent, and keep that frame convention and chart fixed throughout the local ball. Define the square gauge-fixed residual $G_h$ on the $d(M-1)$ interior coordinates by the $(d-1)(M-1)$ scalar entries of $Q_i^T\nabla V(R_i)$ and the $M-1$ independent spacing components $\ell_i-\ell_M$, $1\le i<M$, where $\ell_i=\|R_i-R_{i-1}\|_2$. Its norm is the maximum absolute value of all scalar residual coordinates; the domain norm is the maximum absolute value of all node coordinates. Assume this chosen map is $C^1$ on the open ball in hypothesis 2. The endpoints are fixed and the spacing equations fix the arc-length reparameterization; a zero of this residual is exactly a zero of all centered-tangent normal force components and equality of all segment lengths.

Assume that for all sufficiently small $h$ the following constants $C_0,\beta,L_G,C_I>0$ are independent of $h$:

1. The consistency and interpolation bounds are $\|G_h(z_h)\|_\infty\le C_0h^2$ and $\|I_hz_h-R_*\|_{C^0,\infty}\le C_Ih^2$, where $\|Y\|_{C^0,\infty}:=\sup_{s\in[0,L]}\max_{j<d}|Y_j(s)|$.
2. $DG_h(z_h)$ is invertible with induced maximum-norm inverse bound $\|DG_h(z_h)^{-1}\|_\infty\le\beta$, and $DG_h$ is $L_G$-Lipschitz in the induced maximum operator norm on the open maximum-norm ball of radius $2\rho_h$ about $z_h$, where $\rho_h=2\beta C_0h^2$.
3. That ball lies in the residual's domain and $\beta L_G\rho_h\le1/2$.

Then there is a unique gauge-fixed discrete zero $z_h^*$ in $\overline B_\infty(z_h,\rho_h)$, and

$$\|I_hz_h^*-R_*\|_\infty\le(C_I+2\beta C_0)h^2.$$

The consistency hypothesis is supplied by [[prop-central-string-projected-force-consistency]] for the centered-tangent string residual. The theorem is conditional on the stated uniform inverse and Lipschitz bounds; it proves no blanket convergence result for every potential, mesh, or improved-tangent NEB chain.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The MEP, fixed endpoints, discrete samples, reconstruction, square gauge-fixed residual, and uniform consistency/stability constants in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-regular-minimum-energy-path-in-a-collision-free-tube]]: the continuous path is regular, satisfies the normal-gradient MEP equation, and has fixed endpoints.

[F2] [[prop-central-string-projected-force-consistency]]: on equal arc-length samples the centered-tangent projected force is bounded by a mesh-independent constant times $h^2$.

[F3] [[lem-arc-length-polyline-interpolation-error]]: under its endpoint $C^3$ convention, piecewise-linear interpolation and equal-length redistribution of the sampled smooth path have $O(h^2)$ supremum error.

[F4] [[lem-local-root-in-max-norm]]: if $\beta\epsilon\le r/2$, $\beta L_Gr\le1/2$, and the doubled maximum-norm ball lies in the domain, a square $C^1$ residual with inverse bound $\beta$ and derivative-Lipschitz constant $L_G$ has exactly one zero in the chosen radius-$r$ ball, at distance at most $2\beta\epsilon$.

[F5] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: for each unit frame vector $q$, $|q^Tg|\le\|g\|_2$.

[F6] [[lem-arc-length-polyline-interpolation-error]]: the $C^3$ curve on $[0,L]$ is understood as a restriction from an open interval containing that closed interval, with endpoint derivatives taken continuously from the extension.



**Given:** The hypotheses of the Statement.

## Proof

1.1 The normal frame has $d-1$ columns for each of the $M-1$ interior images, and the $M-1$ independent spacing components add $(d-1)(M-1)+(M-1)=d(M-1)$ scalar residual coordinates, matching the interior-coordinate dimension. [given, algebra]

2.1 The MEP and $C^3$ hypotheses are those in [F1] and [F6]. By [F2], the Euclidean norm of the projected normal force at each sample is bounded by a constant times $h^2$. Each normal coordinate is its inner product with a unit frame vector, so [F5] bounds that scalar by the same amount. By [F3], each chord length satisfies $|\ell_i-h|\le C_1h^3$, so $|\ell_i-\ell_M|\le2C_1h^3\le2C_1h^2$ because $h\le1$. Each scalar coordinate of the residual has a bound independent of the number of images, so their maximum is at most $C_0h^2$ after increasing the uniform constant $C_0$. Also by [F3], the reconstruction of the sample path differs from $R_*$ by at most $C_Ih^2$ in componentwise supremum norm. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 Set $\epsilon_h=\|G_h(z_h)\|_\infty\le C_0h^2$. Apply [F4] in the fixed gauge chart with inverse bound $\beta$, Lipschitz bound $L_G$, and radius $r=\rho_h$. Since $\beta\epsilon_h\le\beta C_0h^2=\rho_h/2$ and $\beta L_G\rho_h\le1/2$, the lemma gives exactly one discrete zero $z_h^*$ in $\overline B_\infty(z_h,\rho_h)$ and $\|z_h^*-z_h\|_\infty\le2\beta\epsilon_h\le\rho_h$. This also covers $\epsilon_h=0$. [F4, given, step 2.1]

4.1 For each curve parameter, piecewise-linear reconstruction is a coordinatewise convex combination of neighboring node values. Hence its componentwise supremum norm is nonexpansive: $\|I_hz_h^*-I_hz_h\|_{C^0,\infty}\le\|z_h^*-z_h\|_\infty\le\rho_h$. The interpolation error in [F3] is stated in Euclidean vector norm and therefore also bounds the componentwise supremum norm. ## Example

On $\mathbb R^2$, let $V(x,y)=x^4/24+y^2/2$, take the point $(0,0)$ and direction $v=e_1$. The exact Hessian action is $\nabla^2V(0,0)e_1=0$. With exact gradients, the central dimer estimate is $D_\epsilon=(\epsilon^2/6)e_1$. If the two gradient evaluations have errors $+\eta e_1$ and $-\eta e_1$, each of norm $\eta$, the computed estimate becomes $\widehat D_\epsilon=(\epsilon^2/6+\eta/\epsilon)e_1$. The truncation bias decreases with $\epsilon$, while this permitted noise contribution increases as $\epsilon$ shrinks.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The potential, point, direction, finite-difference distance $\epsilon>0$, and opposite evaluation errors of magnitude $\eta\ge0$.

[F1] [[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]: the Hessian is the Jacobian of the gradient; at the origin its action on $e_1$ is zero.

[F2] [[lem-dimer-central-force-hessian-vector-error]]: for $C^4$ potentials the paired central gradient difference has truncation error $O(\epsilon^2)$ and force-evaluation contribution at most $\eta/\epsilon$.



**Given:** The data in the Example.

## Proof

1.1 The gradient is $\nabla V(x,y)=(x^3/6,y)$. Thus $\nabla V(\epsilon e_1)=(\epsilon^3/6,0)$ and $\nabla V(-\epsilon e_1)=(-\epsilon^3/6,0)$. Their central difference is $((\epsilon^3/3)/(2\epsilon),0)=(\epsilon^2/6)e_1$. The Hessian at the origin is $\operatorname{diag}(0,1)$, so [F1] gives $He_1=0$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Adding the stated force errors changes the numerator by $2\eta e_1$; division by $2\epsilon$ adds $\eta e_1/\epsilon$. Hence the computed estimate is exactly $\widehat D_\epsilon=(\epsilon^2/6+\eta/\epsilon)e_1$. This realizes both contributions in [F2] for this example. [F2, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 For fixed $\eta>0$, the deterministic term $\epsilon^2/6$ tends to zero as $\epsilon\to0$, but the permitted error term $\eta/\epsilon$ grows without bound. Therefore reducing the dimer separation does not monotonically improve the Hessian-vector estimate when force evaluations are inexact. [step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

## Example

Let $D=(-\pi/4,\pi/4)\times(-1/4,1/4)$ and define

$$X(s,n)=(1+n)(\cos s,\sin s),\qquad U:=X(D).$$

This is an open annular sector: its points have radius $3/4<\|x\|_2<5/4$, positive first coordinate, and angular coordinate in $(-\pi/4,\pi/4)$. The displayed polar map is one-to-one on $D$ with smooth inverse $s=\arctan(y/x)$ and $n=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}-1$. Let $a=\pi/6$, $W(s)=(s^2-a^2)^2$, and define $V(X(s,n))=W(s)+n^2/2$ on $U$. The curve $R(t)=X(-a+2at,0)$, $0\le t\le1$, is a regular MEP joining the two minima $X(-a,0)$ and $X(a,0)$. Its image is the circular arc of radius one. The point $X(0,0)$ is an index-one saddle.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The chart, potential, $a=\pi/6$, and path in the Example.

[F1] [[def-regular-minimum-energy-path-in-a-collision-free-tube]]: a regular MEP has zero gradient component normal to its unit tangent, and the endpoints are fixed data.

[F2] [[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]: at a critical point the Hessian is the matrix of second partial derivatives and its negative-eigenvalue count is the Morse index used here. Since $V$ is $C^2$, [[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]] makes that Hessian symmetric.

[F3] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: derivatives of a scalar field in the displayed chart equal its ambient gradient paired with the chart tangent vectors.

[F4] Since $U$ is open, a sufficiently small convex open ball centered at $X(0,0)$ has its closure in $U$. The potential is $C^\infty$ on that ball, so [[thm-multivariable-taylor-formula-with-lagrange-remainder]] applies there; bounded third derivatives on the compact closure give a quadratic expansion with remainder $O(\|x-X(0,0)\|_2^3)=o(\|x-X(0,0)\|_2^2)$.



**Given:** The data above.

## Proof

1.1 Write $T(s)=(-\sin s,\cos s)$ and $N(s)=(\cos s,\sin s)$. Then $X_s=(1+n)T(s)$ and $X_n=N(s)$ are orthogonal, with lengths $1+n>0$ and $1$. By [F3], $\nabla V(X(s,n))\cdot T(s)=W'(s)/(1+n)$ and $\nabla V(X(s,n))\cdot N(s)=n$. At $n=0$, the path tangent is $T(s)$ and its unit normal is $N(s)$, so the normal gradient component vanishes. The path is regular because $\|R'(t)\|_2=2a>0$; hence it is a regular MEP by [F1]. [F1, F3, given, algebra]

1.2 Since $W(s)\ge0$ and $n^2/2\ge0$, the potential is nonnegative and equals zero exactly at $(s,n)=(-a,0)$ and $(a,0)$. Thus both specified endpoints are global minima on $U$. [given, algebra]

2.1 At $(s,n)=(0,0)$, $W'(0)=0$ and $n=0$, so step 1.1 gives $\nabla V(X(0,0))=0$. The coordinate Hessian of $V\circ X=W(s)+n^2/2$ is $\operatorname{diag}(W''(0),1)=\operatorname{diag}(-4a^2,1)$. By [F4], the quadratic Taylor term of $V$ at $X(0,0)$ is $\frac12v^T(D^2V)v+o(\|v\|_2^2)$. Substituting $v=X(s,n)-X(0,0)=DX(0,0)(s,n)+O(s^2+n^2)$ shows the coordinate quadratic form is $DX(0,0)^T(D^2V)DX(0,0)$; the linear term vanishes because the point is critical. Since $DX(0,0)=[T(0),N(0)]$ is orthogonal, this is an orthogonal representation of the ambient Hessian. By [F2] it has exactly one negative eigenvalue, making the point an index-one saddle. [F2, F4, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 The fixed-endpoint finite-image string of [[alg-finite-image-string-method]] can sample and redistribute this arc, but that finite procedure alone does not imply convergence to it from arbitrary initial images. [given, step 2.1] ∎

## Example

Let $V(x,y)=-x^2-y^2$ on $U=\mathbb R^2$. The origin is a critical point and a strict local maximum, but its Hessian has two negative eigenvalues. [F2] [[thm-local-index-one-saddle-certificate-from-enclosures]]: the nearby-saddle claim requires such an index-one enclosure at the reported point.



**Given:** $V(x,y)=-x^2-y^2$ and the origin.

## Proof

1.1 The gradient is $\nabla V=(-2x,-2y)$, so it vanishes at $(0,0)$; the Hessian is $H=-2I$, with ordered eigenvalues $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=-2$. [given, algebra]

3.1 The point is a maximum with Morse index two, not index one. [F2, step 2.1] ∎

## Example

For each $\delta>0$, let

$$H_\delta=\begin{pmatrix}-\delta&0\\0&\delta\end{pmatrix},\qquad E_\delta=\begin{pmatrix}0&\delta\\\delta&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \widehat H_\delta=H_\delta+E_\delta.$$

The exact lowest eigenvector is $e_1$. The perturbation has Euclidean operator norm $\delta$, which tends to zero with the gap, but the lowest eigenvector of $\widehat H_\delta$ remains at angle $\arctan(\sqrt2-1)>0$ from $e_1$. Thus an absolute perturbation tolerance alone cannot guarantee a mode error tending to zero as the spectral gap collapses.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The matrices above and the mode-separation context in [[thm-dimer-mode-perturbation-and-local-saddle-error]].

[F1] [[thm-dimer-mode-perturbation-and-local-saddle-error]]: the mode-angle bound depends on the error-to-gap ratio, not on absolute error alone.

## Proof

**Given:** $\delta>0$ and the two symmetric matrices in the Example.

1.1 The eigenvalues of $H_\delta$ are $-\delta$ and $\delta$, with exact lowest eigenvector $e_1$ and spectral gap $2\delta$. Also $E_\delta^TE_\delta=\delta^2I$, so its operator norm is $\delta$. [given, algebra]

1.2 The eigenvalues of $\widehat H_\delta$ are $\pm\sqrt2\,\delta$. For the negative eigenvalue, the first row equation gives $(-1+\sqrt2)x+y=0$, so a lowest unit eigenvector is proportional to $(1,1-\sqrt2)$. Its angle with $e_1$ is therefore $\arctan(|1-\sqrt2|)=\arctan(\sqrt2-1)$, a positive constant independent of $\delta$. [given, algebra]

2.1 As $\delta\downarrow0$, the perturbation norm tends to zero while this angle stays fixed at $\arctan(\sqrt2-1)>0$. The spectral gap also tends to zero, so this does not contradict the separated-mode bound [F1]; it shows why that bound must include a gap scale. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Example

Let $U=\mathbb R^2$ and $V\equiv0$. Every regular path from $A=(0,0)$ to $B=(1,0)$ satisfies the MEP equation, so there are infinitely many distinct continuum MEPs. For a finite string with $M=2$, both chains

$$R_1^{(0)}=(1/2,0),\qquad R_1^{(1)}=(1/2,1)$$

have equal adjacent segment lengths and zero projected force. The improved-tangent NEB ordinary force also vanishes for both. Thus their discrete residuals are exactly zero, although their interior images differ.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The zero potential, fixed endpoints $A,B$, two finite chains, and the definitions of the string, NEB, and stable path comparison.

[F1] [[def-regular-minimum-energy-path-in-a-collision-free-tube]]: a regular path is an MEP when the normal gradient vanishes; fixed endpoints are part of the path data.

[F2] [[alg-finite-image-string-method]]: the string stops when the projected-force and equal-spacing residuals are both within tolerance.

[F3] [[alg-improved-tangent-climbing-neb]]: the ordinary NEB force is projected gradient plus a tangential spring term.

[F4] [[thm-gauge-fixed-stable-discrete-path-comparison]]: a local path error conclusion requires an invertible residual Jacobian with a uniform inverse bound and other stated consistency/stability hypotheses.

## Proof

**Given:** The potential, endpoints, and finite chains in the Example.

1.1 For each $c\in\mathbb R$, $R_c(t)=(t,c\sin(\pi t))$ on $[0,1]$ is regular because its first coordinate derivative is $1$, and it has endpoints $A,B$. Since $\nabla V=0$, every normal gradient component is zero, so [F1] makes every $R_c$ an MEP. Distinct $c$ give distinct paths. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 For $M=2$, each listed interior point is equidistant from $A$ and $B$: the two distances are $1/2$ when $R_1=(1/2,0)$ and both $\sqrt{5}/2$ when $R_1=(1/2,1)$. Thus the adjacent lengths agree. Since the gradient is zero, the string projected force is zero by [F2], and the ordinary NEB spring term is also zero by [F3]. Both chains therefore have exactly zero force and spacing residuals. [F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 The two chains differ in their interior image, and the continuum family in step 1.1 is nonunique. In this example the string residual map has no locally invertible Jacobian that can isolate a path: its force components vanish identically and its spacing equation alone cannot determine the two coordinates of the interior image. Hence the stable comparison theorem's inverse/stability premise [F4] is absent, and zero discrete residual does not imply a unique or accurate continuum path. [F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $N\ge2$ and $x_j=2\pi j/N$. If integers $k,r$ satisfy $k\equiv r\pmod N$, then
$$
e^{ikx_j}=e^{irx_j}\qquad(0\le j<N).
$$
Consequently, sampling a product of Fourier modes with frequencies $k_1,\ldots,k_s$ gives the same nodal data as the single mode whose frequency is the sum $\sum_{\ell=1}^s k_\ell$ reduced modulo $N$.

The frequency space in [[def-periodic-fourier-collocation-grid]] is real-valued. For complex data, let $\mathcal T_N^{\mathbb C}$ be the space obtained by allowing complex coefficients in that same real basis, and extend its cardinal formula by
$$
I_N^{\mathbb C}V(x):=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}V_jL_j(x),\qquad V\in\mathbb C^N.
$$
Then $I_N^{\mathbb C}V$ is the unique member of $\mathcal T_N^{\mathbb C}$ with nodal data $V$. On real data this formula agrees with $I_N$; in the even case the complex Nyquist samples are interpolated by the real basis function $\cos(Nx/2)$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An integer $N\ge2$, its periodic grid, and integers $k,r$ with $k-r=qN$ for some integer $q$.

[F1] [[def-periodic-fourier-collocation-grid]]: the grid nodes are $x_j=2\pi j/N$, the cardinal functions are $L_j$, and on the grid the complexified basis modes give one complete residue system modulo $N$ (the even-grid Nyquist cosine has the samples of the residue $N/2$); the complexification and its cardinal formula are specified in the Statement.

[F2] [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]]: $e^{z+w}=e^ze^w$; [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]: $e^w=1$ when $w\in2\pi i\mathbb Z$.

[F3] [[lem-orthogonality-of-characters-on-a-finite-cyclic-group]]: the sum over a complete residue system of the characters at $i-j$ is $N$ when $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise.

[F4] [[thm-finite-fourier-inversion]]: complex nodal data on $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ have a unique finite Fourier representation.

[F5] [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]: $e^{it}=\cos t+i\sin t$ for real $t$.

[F6] [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]] and [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]]: $\sin0=0$ and $\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x$, hence $\sin(m\pi)=0$ for every integer $m$.

## Proof

1.1 Since $k-r=qN$, for every grid index $j$ we have $e^{i(k-r)x_j}=e^{2\pi iqj}=1$ by [F2]. Multiplying by $e^{irx_j}$ gives $e^{ikx_j}=e^{irx_j}$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 For frequencies $k_1,\ldots,k_s$, multiplication of the sampled modes gives $\prod_{\ell=1}^s e^{ik_\ell x_j}=e^{i(\sum_\ell k_\ell)x_j}$ by the exponential addition law in [F2]. Applying step 1.1 to this sum and any congruent representative proves the product aliasing identity. [given, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For $\Delta=x_i-x_j$, Euler's identity [F5] writes the odd-grid kernel as $L_j(x_i)=N^{-1}\sum_{k=-K}^{K}e^{ik\Delta}$ when $N=2K+1$. For an even grid $N=2K$, it writes the kernel as $L_j(x_i)=N^{-1}\sum_{k=-K+1}^{K}e^{ik\Delta}$, because $K\Delta=\pi(i-j)$ and [F6] makes the sine term at this Nyquist frequency vanish. In either branch $e^{iN\Delta}=1$ by [F2], so the sum over these complete residue systems equals the sum over $k=0,\ldots,N-1$. Character orthogonality [F3] therefore gives $L_j(x_i)=1$ for $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise. Hence the displayed complex-linear cardinal formula interpolates every $V\in\mathbb C^N$; uniqueness in [F4] proves it is the unique member of $\mathcal T_N^{\mathbb C}$. The product samples from step 2.1 therefore have that unique interpolant. In the even Nyquist case the interpolant is $\cos(Nx/2)$, not the complex exponential as a function away from the grid. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $N\ge2$, let $U=(U_j)_{j=0}^{N-1}\in\mathbb R^N$, and let $p=I_NU\in\mathcal T_N$ be the interpolant defined in [[def-periodic-fourier-collocation-grid]]. The matrix [[alg-periodic-fourier-collocation-differentiation-matrix]] satisfies
$$
(D_NU)_i=p'(x_i),\qquad 0\le i<N.
$$
For even $N$, this statement includes the Nyquist cosine mode, whose derivative vanishes at the grid nodes.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An integer $N\ge2$, the periodic grid and interpolant, and real nodal data $U$.

[F1] [[def-periodic-fourier-collocation-grid]]: $I_NU=\sum_jU_jL_j$ on the $N$ equally spaced nodes; its frequency set is a complete set of residues modulo $N$, with only the cosine Nyquist mode when $N$ is even.

[F2] [[alg-periodic-fourier-collocation-differentiation-matrix]]: $(D_N)_{ij}$ is the termwise derivative of $L_j$ evaluated at $x_i$; in the even case the Nyquist sine term is zero at these nodes.

[F3] [[lem-orthogonality-of-characters-on-a-finite-cyclic-group]]: summing all $N$ characters over $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ gives $N$ when the two indices agree modulo $N$ and $0$ otherwise.

[F4] [[thm-finite-fourier-inversion]]: the finite Fourier transform on $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ has an inverse, so the frequency coefficients representing nodal data are unique.

[F5] [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]]: $(\cos kx)'=-k\sin(kx)$ and $(\sin kx)'=k\cos(kx)$.

[F6] [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]: $e^{it}=\cos t+i\sin t$ for real $t$.

[F7] [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]]: $\sin(k\pi)=0$ for every integer $k$.

[F8] [[thm-sine-and-cosine-subtraction-formulas]]: $\cos(u-v)=\cos u\cos v+\sin u\sin v$, so each $\cos(k(x-x_j))$ expands into cosine and sine modes with frequency $k$.

[F9] [[thm-chain-rule]]: differentiating a trigonometric function composed with $x\mapsto k(x-x_j)$ multiplies its derivative by $k$.

## Proof
1.1 By [F8], each low-frequency cosine difference in $L_j$ expands into the corresponding cosine/sine modes in $\mathcal T_N$. For even $N=2K$, its Nyquist term expands into $\cos(Kx)\cos(Kx_j)+\sin(Kx)\sin(Kx_j)$; [F7] makes the second coefficient zero because $Kx_j=\pi j$. At a grid difference $x_i-x_j=2\pi(i-j)/N$, Euler's identity [F6] rewrites the cosine sum defining $L_j(x_i)$ as the normalized sum of all characters in a complete residue system modulo $N$: for odd $N=2K+1$ the residues are $-K,\ldots,K$, and for even $N=2K$ they are $-K+1,\ldots,K$. Character orthogonality [F3] gives $L_j(x_i)=1$ when $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise. Thus $I_NU$ takes the prescribed nodal values and lies in $\mathcal T_N$. [F1, F3, F6, F7, F8, algebra]

1.2 The space $\mathcal T_N$ has exactly $N$ real basis modes. If two members agree at the $N$ nodes, their difference has zero nodal Fourier transform; inversion [F4] forces every frequency coefficient to vanish, so the interpolant is unique. [F1, F4, algebra]

2.1 Differentiate the finite sum $p(x)=\sum_jU_jL_j(x)$ term by term. By [F5] and [F9], $p'(x_i)=\sum_jU_jL_j'(x_i)$. When $N$ is odd this is exactly the sine sum defining $D_NU$ in [F2]. When $N=2K$ the derivative of the remaining Nyquist term is proportional to $\sin(K(x_i-x_j))=\sin(\pi(i-j))=0$ by [F7], so the same equality holds with the Nyquist term omitted. [F2, F5, F7, F9, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Steps 1.1–2.1 establish the nodal interpolation and derivative identity for every data vector, including both parity branches of $N$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $N\ge1$, let $x_j=\cos(j\pi/N)$, and let $I_N^L$ denote degree-at-most-$N$ interpolation on these nodes. For every integer $n\ge0$, let $\rho_N(n)$ be the unique integer $r\in\{0,\ldots,N\}$ congruent to either $n$ or $-n$ modulo $2N$. Then
$$
I_N^L T_n=T_{\rho_N(n)}.
$$
In particular, sampling a Chebyshev series on the Lobatto grid can fold every degree $n>N$ to a degree at most $N$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An integer $N\ge1$, its Chebyshev–Gauss–Lobatto grid, and an integer $n\ge0$.

[F1] [[def-chebyshev-gauss-lobatto-collocation-grid]]: $x_j=\cos(j\pi/N)$ for $0\le j\le N$, with distinct nodes.

[F2] [[def-chebyshev-polynomials-first-and-second-kind]] defines the polynomials $T_n$; [[thm-chebyshev-multiple-angle-identities]] gives $T_n(\cos\theta)=\cos(n\theta)$.

[F3] [[thm-cardinal-polynomial-interpolant-exists-uniquely]]: a polynomial of degree at most $N$ that agrees with the data at the $N+1$ distinct increasing nodes is their unique interpolant; reversing node order and data order preserves the same interpolation polynomial.

[F4] [[lem-chebyshev-degree-leading-coefficients-and-extreme-values]]: $T_r$ has degree $r$ for every $r\ge1$, and $T_0=1$.

[F5] [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]]: cosine has period $2\pi$ and is even, so $\cos(\alpha+2q\pi)=\cos\alpha$ and $\cos(-\alpha)=\cos\alpha$ for integers $q$.

## Proof

1.1 Reduce $n$ modulo $2N$ to a residue $s\in\{0,\ldots,2N-1\}$ and put $r=\min(s,2N-s)$. Then $0\le r\le N$, $r\equiv n$ or $-n\pmod{2N}$, and this $r$ is unique: the classes $\{\pm r\}$ are distinct for $0<r<N$, with singleton classes at $r=0,N$. [given, F1, choose, algebra]

2.1 For every node $x_j$, [F2] gives $T_n(x_j)=\cos(nj\pi/N)$. Since $n\equiv\pm r\pmod{2N}$, [F5] gives $\cos(nj\pi/N)=\cos(rj\pi/N)=T_r(x_j)$. Thus $T_n$ and $T_r$ have the same nodal values. [F2, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F4], $T_r$ has degree $r\le N$. Interpolation uniqueness [F3] therefore gives $I_N^LT_n=T_r$. [F1, F3, F4, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $N\ge1$, let $U_j\in\mathbb R$ be data on the nodes $x_j=\cos(j\pi/N)$, and let $p$ be the unique polynomial of degree at most $N$ with $p(x_j)=U_j$. The matrix [[alg-chebyshev-gauss-lobatto-differentiation-matrix]] satisfies
$$
(D_NU)_i=p'(x_i),\qquad 0\le i\le N.
$$
In particular, applying $D_N$ twice gives $p''(x_i)$ at each node.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $N\ge1$, distinct Chebyshev–Gauss–Lobatto nodes, and real nodal data.

[F1] [[def-chebyshev-gauss-lobatto-collocation-grid]]: the nodes are distinct; reversing their order gives increasing nodes $z_k=x_{N-k}$.

[F2] [[alg-chebyshev-gauss-lobatto-differentiation-matrix]]: $D_{ij}=\ell_{N-j}'(x_i)$ for the cardinal polynomials of the increasing reindexing.

[F3] [[thm-cardinal-polynomial-interpolant-exists-uniquely]]: at $N+1$ distinct ordered nodes, the cardinal sum is the unique polynomial of degree at most $N$ with the prescribed values.

## Proof

1.1 Reindex the data by $Y_k=U_{N-k}$. By [F1], the nodes $z_k=x_{N-k}$ are strictly increasing, so [F3] gives $p(x)=\sum_{k=0}^NY_k\ell_k(x)$ as the unique degree-at-most-$N$ interpolant. Reversing the finite sum back to the descending index gives $p(x)=\sum_{j=0}^NU_j\ell_{N-j}(x)$. [given, F1, F3, construct]

2.1 Differentiate the finite polynomial sum in step 1.1 term by term. At $x_i$ this gives $p'(x_i)=\sum_{j=0}^NU_j\ell_{N-j}'(x_i)=\sum_{j=0}^N(D_N)_{ij}U_j=(D_NU)_i$ by [F2]. This proves the first identity for each node. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The polynomial $p'$ has degree at most $N-1\le N$ and its nodal values are $D_NU$ by step 2.1. Uniqueness [F3] therefore makes $p'$ the interpolant of the vector $D_NU$. Applying the already proved first-derivative identity of step 2.1 to that vector gives $D_N(D_NU)=(p''(x_i))_{i=0}^N$. [F1, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For the algorithm [[alg-chebyshev-dirichlet-bvp-collocation-boundary-elimination]], a success output is the unique nodal vector with $U_0=g_+$, $U_N=g_-$ satisfying
$$
-(D_N^{(2)}U)_i+a(x_i)(D_NU)_i+b(x_i)U_i=f(x_i),\qquad 1\le i<N,
$$
where $D_N$ is the exact Chebyshev–Gauss–Lobatto differentiation matrix and $D_N^{(2)}=D_ND_N$. If the interior matrix is singular, the algorithm returns singular-interior-matrix and makes no claim about existence or uniqueness for the given right-hand side.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An integer $N\ge2$, node values of $a,b,f$, endpoints $g_-,g_+$, the boundary-elimination algorithm, and its interior matrix $A$.

[F1] [[alg-chebyshev-dirichlet-bvp-collocation-boundary-elimination]]: $C_{ij}=-(D_N^2)_{ij}+a(x_i)(D_N)_{ij}+b(x_i)\delta_{ij}$, $A=(C_{ij})_{1\le i,j<N}$, and $r_i=f(x_i)-C_{i0}g_+-C_{iN}g_-$.

[F2] [[thm-chebyshev-gauss-lobatto-differentiation-is-exact]]: for the interpolant $p$ through the full nodal vector $U$, $D_NU=(p'(x_i))_i$; applying $D_N$ again gives $(p''(x_i))_i$.

[F3] [[thm-invertible-matrix-theorem]]: an invertible square matrix has exactly one solution for every right-hand side.

## Proof
1.1 On a success branch the algorithm sets $U_0=g_+$ and $U_N=g_-$ and solves $AU_I=r$ for the interior vector $U_I=(U_1,\ldots,U_{N-1})$. [given, F1]

1.2 By [F2], $D_NU$ and $D_N^{(2)}U$ are respectively the first and second derivatives of the degree-at-most-$N$ nodal interpolant evaluated at the nodes. [given, F2]

2.1 Expanding the $i$th row of the full expression using [F1] gives $\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}C_{ij}U_j+C_{i0}g_++C_{iN}g_-=f(x_i),$ which is exactly the reduced equation $AU_I=r$ with the definition of $r_i$. Combined with step 1.2, this is the stated collocation equation at every interior node. [given, F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 Since the success branch has invertible $A$, [F3] gives exactly one interior vector solving $AU_I=r$. The prescribed endpoint values then give exactly one full nodal vector. The singular branch returns its declared status and asserts nothing about solvability of its right-hand side. [given, F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Steps 1.1–2.2 prove the success claim and the stated singular-matrix limit. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

Under the pairing of [[def-chebyshev-arcsine-weighted-l2-pairing]],
$$\langle T_m,T_n\rangle_C= \begin{cases} \pi,&m=n=0,\\ \pi/2,&m=n\ge1,\\ 0,&m\ne n. \end{cases}$$
The polynomials $T_0,T_1,\ldots$ form a basis of the real polynomial space, and the pairing is positive definite on continuous real functions on $[-1,1]$. If a continuous real function $h$ satisfies $\langle h,T_n\rangle_C=0$ for every $n\ge0$, then $h=0$ on $[-1,1]$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Natural numbers $m,n$, the Chebyshev polynomials $T_k$, and the arcsine-weighted pairing.

[F1] [[def-chebyshev-arcsine-weighted-l2-pairing]]: $\langle f,g\rangle_C=\int_0^\pi f(\cos\theta)g(\cos\theta)\,d\theta$.

[F2] [[thm-chebyshev-multiple-angle-identities]]: $T_k(\cos\theta)=\cos(k\theta)$ for every natural $k$ and real $\theta$.

[F3] [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]]: $2\cos u\cos v=\cos(u+v)+\cos(u-v)$.

[F4] [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]] and [[thm-ftc-second-part]]: for nonzero integer $k$, $\int_0^\pi\cos(k\theta)\,d\theta=(\sin(k\pi)-\sin0)/k$.

[F5] [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]]: $\sin\pi=0$ and $\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x$, so $\sin(k\pi)=0$ for every integer $k$; [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]]: cosine is even.

[F6] [[def-chebyshev-polynomials-first-and-second-kind]]: $T_0=1$, $T_1=X$, and $T_{n+1}=2XT_n-T_{n-1}$ for $n\ge1$.

[F7] [[cor-weierstrass-approximation-on-a-closed-interval]]: every continuous real function on $[-1,1]$ is a uniform limit of polynomials.

[F8] [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and [[thm-extreme-value-r]]: a continuous real function on $[-1,1]$ is bounded.

[F9] [[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]]: for continuous functions on a compact interval, pointwise lower and upper bounds pass to their integrals.

## Proof
1.1 By [F1]–[F2], $\langle T_m,T_n\rangle_C=\int_0^\pi\cos(m\theta)\cos(n\theta)\,d\theta$. If $m\ne n$, [F3], cosine parity [F5], and $\sin(k\pi)=0$ from [F5] make the integral of each nonzero-frequency cosine vanish by [F4]. If $m=n\ge1$, [F3] gives $\frac12(1+\cos(2m\theta))$, whose integral is $\pi/2$. If $m=n=0$, the integrand is $1$ and its integral is $\pi$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

2.1 The recurrence [F6] shows inductively that $T_n$ has degree $n$ and nonzero leading coefficient: this holds for $T_0,T_1$, and the leading term of $2XT_n$ cannot cancel with the lower-degree $T_{n-1}$. Eliminating the leading term of any polynomial successively proves that $T_0,T_1,\ldots$ span all polynomials; their distinct degrees also give linear independence. Step 1.1 gives positive squared norms and pairwise orthogonality. [F6, step 1.1, algebra, induction]

3.1 Suppose continuous $h$ pairs to zero with every $T_n$. By step 2.1 it pairs to zero with every polynomial. Fix $\varepsilon>0$ and choose a polynomial $q$ with $\|q-h\|_\infty<\varepsilon$ by [F7]. The bound $M=\|h\|_\infty<\infty$ follows from [F8]. The pointwise bounds $-M\varepsilon\le h(\cos\theta)(h-q)(\cos\theta)\le M\varepsilon$ and [F9] give $0\le\langle h,h\rangle_C=\langle h,h-q\rangle_C\le\pi M\varepsilon.$ The lower inequality uses the nonnegative integrand $h(\cos\theta)^2$ and [F9]. Since this holds for every $\varepsilon>0$, $\langle h,h\rangle_C=0$. If $h(x_0)\ne0$ at some $x_0\in[-1,1]$, choose $\theta_0\in[0,\pi]$ with $\cos\theta_0=x_0$; continuity makes $h(\cos\theta)^2$ bounded below by a positive constant on a one-sided neighborhood if $\theta_0$ is an endpoint, or a two-sided neighborhood otherwise. [F9] then gives a positive integral, contradicting zero norm. Therefore $h=0$. [F1, F7, F8, F9, step 2.1, choose, algebra]

4.1 For any continuous $h$, if $\langle h,h\rangle_C=0$ but $h(\cos\theta_0)\ne0$ at some $\theta_0\in[0,\pi]$, continuity gives a one-sided interval at an endpoint, or a two-sided interval in the interior, on which $h(\cos\theta)^2$ is bounded below by a positive number. [F9] makes its integral positive, a contradiction. Thus $h(\cos\theta)=0$ for every $\theta$, and cosine maps $[0,\pi]$ onto $[-1,1]$, so $h=0$. Symmetry and bilinearity follow from the integral definition [F1], proving positive definiteness. [F1, F9, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $s\ge0$, $N\ge0$, and $u\in H_C^s$ as defined in [[def-chebyshev-weighted-spectral-sobolev-scale]]. Then
$$
\|u-\Pi_Nu\|_C\le (1+(N+1)^2)^{-s/2}\|u\|_{H_C^s}.
$$
Thus the weighted projection error is $O(N^{-s})$ when the data belong to this explicitly defined weighted spectral Sobolev space.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $s\ge0$, an integer $N\ge0$, and a Chebyshev coefficient expansion $u=\sum_{n\ge0}c_nT_n$ with finite $H_C^s$ norm.

[F1] [[def-chebyshev-weighted-spectral-sobolev-scale]]: $\Pi_Nu=\sum_{n=0}^Nc_nT_n$ and the $H_C^s$ norm weights coefficient $c_n$ by $(1+n^2)^s$.

[F2] [[lem-chebyshev-polynomials-orthogonal-in-arcsine-weight]]: the squared $C$-norm of $T_0$ is $\pi$ and that of each $T_n$, $n\ge1$, is $\pi/2$.

## Proof
1.1 By [F1], $u-\Pi_Nu=\sum_{n>N}c_nT_n$. Orthogonality from [F2] gives $\|u-\Pi_Nu\|_C^2=\frac{\pi}{2}\sum_{n>N}|c_n|^2.$ Since $n>N$ implies $(1+n^2)^s\ge(1+(N+1)^2)^s$, this is at most $(1+(N+1)^2)^{-s}\frac{\pi}{2}\sum_{n>N}(1+n^2)^s|c_n|^2 \le(1+(N+1)^2)^{-s}\|u\|_{H_C^s}^2.$ Taking square roots proves the result for finite sums. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Finite sums are dense in the completion defining $H_C^s$. The truncation $\Pi_N$ is a contraction in the coefficient norm and in the $C$-norm, so both sides of the finite-sum inequality pass to the limit along any Cauchy sequence of finite sums. This yields the stated estimate for every $u\in H_C^s$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For $f\in C[-1,1]$ and $N\ge0$, let $E_N(f)$ and $\Lambda_N^L$ be the best uniform error and the Lebesgue constant from [[def-best-uniform-polynomial-approximation-error-and-chebyshev-interpolants]]. Then
$$
\|f-I_N^Lf\|_C\le \sqrt{\pi}\,(1+\Lambda_N^L)E_N(f),
$$
where $\|\cdot\|_C$ is the arcsine-weighted norm of [[def-chebyshev-arcsine-weighted-l2-pairing]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A continuous real function $f$ on $[-1,1]$ and $N\ge0$.

[F1] [[thm-chebyshev-interpolation-near-best-error-bound]]: $\|f-I_N^Lf\|_\infty\le(1+\Lambda_N^L)E_N(f)$.

[F2] [[def-chebyshev-arcsine-weighted-l2-pairing]]: $\|h\|_C^2=\int_0^\pi|h(\cos\theta)|^2d\theta$, so $\|h\|_C\le\sqrt{\pi}\|h\|_\infty$.

## Proof
1.1 For every $\theta\in[0,\pi]$, $|h(\cos\theta)|\le\|h\|_\infty$. Integrating its square in [F2] gives $\|h\|_C^2\le\pi\|h\|_\infty^2$ and hence $\|h\|_C\le\sqrt{\pi}\|h\|_\infty$. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 Apply step 1.1 to $h=f-I_N^Lf$, then use the uniform near-best bound [F1]. The result is $\|f-I_N^Lf\|_C\le\sqrt{\pi}(1+\Lambda_N^L)E_N(f)$. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $s>1/2$, $N\ge1$, and $u=\sum_{n\ge0}c_nT_n\in H_C^s$. Then the series converges uniformly, its nodal interpolant $I_N^Lu$ is defined, and
$$\|u-I_N^Lu\|_C\le C_sN^{-s}\|u\|_{H_C^s},\qquad C_s=1+2\sqrt{1+\frac1{2s-1}}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A real $s>1/2$, an integer $N\ge1$, and a Chebyshev coefficient sequence in $H_C^s$.

[F1] [[def-chebyshev-weighted-spectral-sobolev-scale]]: $\|u\|_{H_C^s}^2=\pi|c_0|^2+\frac\pi2\sum_{n\ge1}(1+n^2)^s|c_n|^2$.

[F2] [[lem-chebyshev-lobatto-mode-aliasing]]: $I_N^LT_n=T_{\rho_N(n)}$ for the unique folded degree $\rho_N(n)\in\{0,\ldots,N\}$.

[F3] [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]]: $I_N^Lf$ is the finite Lagrange cardinal sum at the $N+1$ distinct Lobatto nodes, hence is linear and continuous in the uniform norm.

[F4] [[lem-chebyshev-polynomials-orthogonal-in-arcsine-weight]]: $\|T_0\|_C^2=\pi$ and $\|T_r\|_C^2=\pi/2$ for $r\ge1$, with distinct modes orthogonal.

[F5] [[thm-chebyshev-multiple-angle-identities]] and [[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]]: $T_n(\cos\theta)=\cos(n\theta)$ and $|\cos t|\le1$ for real $t$.

[F6] [[lem-ltwo-fourier-decay-implies-absolute-convergence-by-cauchy-schwarz]]: for $s>1/2$, a sequence with $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}(1+|k|)^{2s}|a_k|^2<\infty$ is absolutely summable.

[F7] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]]: for finite real lists, $|\sum a_kb_k|^2\le(\sum a_k^2)(\sum b_k^2)$.

## Proof

1.1 Put $a_n=c_n$ for $n\ge0$ and $a_n=0$ for negative $n$. By [F1], $\sum_{n\ge0}(1+n^2)^s|c_n|^2<\infty$; since $(1+n)^{2s}\le2^s(1+n^2)^s$, [F6] gives $\sum_{n\ge0}|c_n|<\infty$. By [F5], $|T_n(x)|\le1$ on $[-1,1]$, so the series converges uniformly and its nodal values are defined. [given, F1, F5, F6, algebra]

2.1 Write $u=S_N+R_N$, where $S_N=\sum_{n=0}^Nc_nT_n$ and $R_N=\sum_{n>N}c_nT_n$. The Lagrange operator [F3] reproduces $S_N$ and is continuous in the uniform norm; therefore $u-I_N^Lu=R_N-I_N^LR_N$. By [F2], uniform convergence and the finite cardinal sum give $I_N^LR_N=\sum_{r=0}^Nb_rT_r$, where $b_r=\sum_{n>N:\rho_N(n)=r}c_n$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Fix $r\in\{0,\ldots,N\}$. Since $n\equiv r$ or $-r\pmod{2N}$, every index in its alias class has form $2qN+r$ or $2qN-r$. When $n>N$ the corresponding integer $q$ is positive. For each $q$ there are at most two candidates; the plus candidate is at least $qN$, and the minus candidate is at least $(2q-1)N\ge qN$. Hence $\sum_{n>N:\rho_N(n)=r}(1+n^2)^{-s}\le2N^{-2s}\sum_{q\ge1}q^{-2s}\le2\left(1+\frac1{2s-1}\right)N^{-2s}.$ The last inequality separates the $q=1$ term and bounds the decreasing tail by $\int_1^\infty x^{-2s}\,dx$. [given, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Let $A_s=1+1/(2s-1)$. Apply [F7] to finite partial sums over an alias class, use step 3.1, and pass to the limit; the coefficient sums converge absolutely by step 1.1. This gives $|b_r|^2\le2A_sN^{-2s}\sum_{n>N:\rho_N(n)=r}(1+n^2)^s|c_n|^2.$ The alias classes partition $n>N$. By [F4], $\|I_N^LR_N\|_C^2\le\pi\sum_{r=0}^N|b_r|^2\le2\pi A_sN^{-2s}\sum_{n>N}(1+n^2)^s|c_n|^2\le4A_sN^{-2s}\|u\|_{H_C^s}^2,$ where the last inequality uses [F1]. Also [F1] and [F4] give $\|R_N\|_C^2=\frac\pi2\sum_{n>N}|c_n|^2\le(N+1)^{-2s}\|u\|_{H_C^s}^2.$ Thus $\|R_N\|_C\le(N+1)^{-s}\|u\|_{H_C^s}$. [F1, F2, F4, F7, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 By step 2.1 and the triangle inequality, $\|u-I_N^Lu\|_C\le\|R_N\|_C+\|I_N^LR_N\|_C\le(1+2\sqrt{A_s})N^{-s}\|u\|_{H_C^s}$ because $(N+1)^{-s}\le N^{-s}$. This is the claimed estimate. [step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $N\ge1$ and $f\in C^{N+1}([-1,1])$. Let $I_N^Lf$ be interpolation at the nodes $x_j=\cos(j\pi/N)$. Then
$$\|f-I_N^Lf\|_C \le \sqrt{\pi}\,\frac{2^{1-N}}{(N+1)!}\max_{x\in[-1,1]}|f^{(N+1)}(x)|.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $N\ge1$ and $f\in C^{N+1}([-1,1])$.

[F1] [[def-chebyshev-gauss-lobatto-collocation-grid]]: the $N+1$ distinct nodes are $x_j=\cos(j\pi/N)$, including both endpoints.

[F2] [[def-chebyshev-polynomials-first-and-second-kind]] and [[lem-chebyshev-degree-leading-coefficients-and-extreme-values]]: $T_N$ has degree $N$ and leading coefficient $2^{N-1}$ for $N\ge1$.

[F3] [[thm-chebyshev-multiple-angle-identities]], [[thm-chain-rule]], and [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]]: for $x=\cos\theta$, $0<\theta<\pi$, $T_N'(x)=N\sin(N\theta)/\sin\theta$.

[F4] [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]]: $\sin(k\pi)=0$ for every integer $k$, by repeated shifts by $\pi$.

[F5] [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]]: $|\sin t|\le1$ for every real $t$.

[F6] [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]]: the node polynomial is $\omega_N(x)=\prod_{j=0}^N(x-x_j)$ and $I_N^Lf$ is its degree-at-most-$N$ Lagrange interpolant after reversing the decreasing node order.

[F7] [[thm-lagrange-interpolation-remainder]]: for $x$ off the nodes, $f(x)-I_N^Lf(x)=f^{(N+1)}(\xi)\omega_N(x)/(N+1)!$ for some $\xi$ in the interval between the extreme nodes and $x$; at a node the error is zero.

[F8] [[def-chebyshev-arcsine-weighted-l2-pairing]]: $\|h\|_C\le\sqrt{\pi}\|h\|_\infty$ because the angular measure has total mass $\pi$.

[F9] [[def-higher-derivatives-and-smoothness]], [[thm-heine-borel-r]], and [[thm-extreme-value-r]]: $f^{(N+1)}$ is continuous on the compact interval, so the displayed finite maximum exists.

[F10] [[thm-nonzero-real-polynomial-has-at-most-degree-many-distinct-roots]]: a polynomial with more distinct roots than its degree is the zero polynomial.

## Proof
1.1 By the recurrence in [F2], $T_N$ has leading coefficient $2^{N-1}$ for every $N\ge1$. Hence $q_N(x):=\frac{2^{1-N}}{N}(x^2-1)T_N'(x)$ is monic of degree $N+1$. [F2, algebra]

1.2 For $1\le j<N$, put $\theta_j=j\pi/N$. Then [F3] and [F4] give $T_N'(x_j)=N\sin(j\pi)/\sin\theta_j=0$. Also $q_N(1)=q_N(-1)=0$. Thus $q_N$ vanishes at all $N+1$ distinct nodes in [F1]. The node product $\omega_N$ is also monic of degree $N+1$ by [F6]; their difference has degree at most $N$ and $N+1$ distinct roots, so [F10] gives $q_N=\omega_N$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F6, F10, algebra]

2.1 For $x=\cos\theta$ with $0<\theta<\pi$, the derivative formula in [F3] gives $|\omega_N(x)|=2^{1-N}|\sin\theta\,\sin(N\theta)|\le2^{1-N}.$ The inequality uses [F5]. At the endpoints $\omega_N=0$, so this bound holds on all of $[-1,1]$. [F1, F3, F5, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 At nodes the interpolation error is zero; off the nodes apply [F7] and step 2.1. Since the maximum in [F9] is finite, this gives $\|f-I_N^Lf\|_\infty\le \frac{2^{1-N}}{(N+1)!}\max_{[-1,1]}|f^{(N+1)}|.$ [F1, F7, F9, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Apply the weighted-norm estimate [F8] to the uniform error in step 3.1. This proves the stated inequality. [F8, step 3.1, algebra] ∎
