## Statement

Let $\rho>1$, and let $E_\rho$ be the closed Bernstein ellipse
$$
E_\rho=\left\{\frac{\rho e^{it}+\rho^{-1}e^{-it}}2:0\le t\le2\pi\right\}
$$
together with its interior. Suppose $f$ is real-valued on $[-1,1]$, extends holomorphically to an open neighborhood of $E_\rho$, and satisfies $|f(z)|\le M$ on $E_\rho$. Then for every $N\ge1$,
$$
\|f-I_N^Lf\|_C\le \frac{4\sqrt{\pi}M}{\rho-1}\rho^{-N}.
$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\rho>1$, a function $f$ holomorphic near $E_\rho$ with $|f|\le M$ there, and $N\ge1$.

[F1] [[thm-cauchy-theorem-one-exceptional-point-on-a-star-shaped-domain]]: a holomorphic function on a star-shaped open set has zero integral around every closed rectifiable contour in that set.

[F2] [[thm-chebyshev-multiple-angle-identities]] and [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]]: $T_n(\cos\theta)=\cos(n\theta)$ and cosine is even and $2\pi$-periodic.

[F3] [[lem-chebyshev-lobatto-mode-aliasing]]: $I_N^LT_n=T_{\rho_N(n)}$ for the folded degree $0\le\rho_N(n)\le N$.

[F4] [[lem-chebyshev-polynomials-orthogonal-in-arcsine-weight]]: the coefficient convention is $c_0=\pi^{-1}\int_0^\pi f(\cos\theta)d\theta$, $c_n=2\pi^{-1}\int_0^\pi f(\cos\theta)\cos(n\theta)d\theta$ for $n\ge1$, and a continuous function with all Chebyshev coefficients zero is zero.

[F5] [[def-chebyshev-arcsine-weighted-l2-pairing]]: the angular measure has total mass $\pi$, so $\|h\|_C\le\sqrt\pi\|h\|_\infty$.

[F6] [[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]]: $|\cos t|\le1$ for real $t$.

[F7] [[thm-geometric-series]]: for $r\in\mathbb R$ with $|r|<1$, $\sum_{k\ge0}r^k=1/(1-r)$.

## Proof

1.1 For $z=\theta-it$ with $0\le t\le\log\rho$, $\cos z=\cos\theta\cosh t+i\sin\theta\sinh t.$ For fixed $t>0$, its real and imaginary parts satisfy $x^2/\cosh^2t+y^2/\sinh^2t=1$, so the image is the Bernstein ellipse with parameter $e^t$; these ellipses are nested. Since $f$ is holomorphic on a neighborhood of $E_\rho$, $g(z):=f(\cos z)$ is holomorphic on an open strip containing the rectangle $-\pi\le\Re z\le\pi$, $-\log\rho\le\Im z\le0$. On its lower edge $|g(\theta-i\log\rho)|\le M$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 For $n\ge1$, set $H_n(z)=g(z)e^{-inz}$. It is holomorphic on that strip and $2\pi$-periodic. Apply [F1] to the boundary of the rectangle with vertices $-\pi,\pi,\pi-i\log\rho,-\pi-i\log\rho$. The vertical integrals cancel by periodicity, so the top and lower horizontal integrals, both oriented from left to right, are equal. By [F2] and evenness, the coefficient in [F4] is $c_n=\frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}g(\theta)e^{-in\theta}\,d\theta.$ On the lower edge, $|e^{-in(\theta-i\log\rho)}|=\rho^{-n}$, so the shifted integral gives $|c_n|\le2M\rho^{-n}$. Also [F4] and $|f|\le M$ give $|c_0|\le M$. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The coefficient bounds in step 2.1 make $\sum_{n\ge0}c_nT_n$ uniformly convergent, since [F2] and [F6] give $|T_n(x)|\le1$. Uniform convergence permits termwise integration against each bounded $T_k$; orthogonality [F4] shows that this series and $f$ have the same Chebyshev coefficients. Their continuous difference therefore has every coefficient zero, so [F4] gives $f=\sum_{n\ge0}c_nT_n$ on $[-1,1]$. [F2, F4, F6, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By [F3], every mode $T_n$ with $n>N$ interpolates to a Chebyshev mode. Each such mode has sup norm at most one by [F2] and [F6]. Thus the series tail and its interpolant each have sup norm at most $\sum_{n>N}|c_n|$, and $\|f-I_N^Lf\|_\infty\le2\sum_{n>N}|c_n|\le4M\sum_{n>N}\rho^{-n}=\frac{4M}{\rho-1}\rho^{-N},$ where [F7] evaluates the geometric tail. [F2, F3, F6, F7, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Apply [F5] to the uniform error in step 4.1. This yields $\|f-I_N^Lf\|_C\le4\sqrt\pi M(\rho-1)^{-1}\rho^{-N}$, as claimed. [F5, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $N\ge0$, let $M\ge2$ be even, put $h=\pi/M$, and let $G_{ij}=\langle T_i,T_j\rangle_C$ be the exact weighted mass entry from [[def-chebyshev-arcsine-weighted-l2-pairing]]. The approximation $M^S_{ij}$ from [[alg-chebyshev-composite-simpson-weighted-mass-matrix]] satisfies
$$
|G_{ij}-M^S_{ij}|\le \frac{\pi h^4}{180}(i+j)^4,\qquad 0\le i,j\le N.
$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Integers $N\ge0$, even $M\ge2$, $h=\pi/M$, and indices $0\le i,j\le N$.

[F1] [[def-chebyshev-arcsine-weighted-l2-pairing]]: $\langle T_i,T_j\rangle_C=\int_0^\pi T_i(\cos\theta)T_j(\cos\theta)\,d\theta$.

[F2] [[alg-chebyshev-composite-simpson-weighted-mass-matrix]]: $M^S_{ij}$ is the composite Simpson value on $[0,\pi]$ for $g_{ij}(\theta)=T_i(\cos\theta)T_j(\cos\theta)$ with step $h$.

[F3] [[thm-composite-simpson-error-bound]]: if $g\in C^4([0,\pi])$, then $|\int_0^\pi g-Q_S(g;0,\pi,M)|\le \pi h^4\max|g^{(4)}|/180$.

[F4] [[thm-chebyshev-multiple-angle-identities]] and [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]]: $T_k(\cos\theta)=\cos(k\theta)$ and $2\cos u\cos v=\cos(u+v)+\cos(u-v)$.

[F5] [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]]: differentiating $\cos(k\theta)$ four times multiplies it by $k^4$.

## Proof
1.1 By [F4], $g_{ij}(\theta)=\tfrac12\{\cos((i+j)\theta)+\cos((i-j)\theta)\}.$ This finite trigonometric expression is $C^4$ on $[0,\pi]$. Its fourth derivative is $g_{ij}^{(4)}(\theta)=\tfrac12\{(i+j)^4\cos((i+j)\theta)+(i-j)^4\cos((i-j)\theta)\},$ by four applications of [F5]. Therefore $\max_{[0,\pi]}|g_{ij}^{(4)}|\le\tfrac12((i+j)^4+|i-j|^4)\le(i+j)^4.$ This also covers $i=j=0$, when the fourth derivative is zero. [given, F4, F5, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F3] to $g_{ij}$ and use [F1]–[F2] to identify the exact integral and the Simpson approximation. The derivative bound in step 1.1 gives the claimed entrywise error. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Under the hypotheses of [[def-weighted-orthogonal-polynomial-galerkin-space]], for every real measurable $u$ such that $\int|u p_j|\,d\mu<\infty$ for $0\le j\le N$, the formula
$$
\Pi_Nu=\sum_{j=0}^{N}\frac{\int u(x)p_j(x)\,d\mu(x)}{h_j}\,p_j
$$
is finite and defines the unique element of $V_N(\mu)$ whose residual is orthogonal to every $p_i$, $0\le i\le N$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite positive measure $\mu$ with the support condition in [[def-weighted-orthogonal-polynomial-galerkin-space]], an integer $N\ge0$, and a real measurable $u$ with $\int|u p_j|\,d\mu<\infty$ for $0\le j\le N$.

[F1] [[def-weighted-orthogonal-polynomial-galerkin-space]]: the basis polynomials $p_0,\ldots,p_N$ are monic orthogonal polynomials and $h_j=\int p_j^2\,d\mu>0$.

[F2] [[thm-gauss-polynomial-moment-pairing-is-an-inner-product]]: on each finite polynomial space allowed by the moment data, the moment pairing is a positive-definite real inner product.

[F3] The given integrability hypotheses make each numerator $\int u p_j\,d\mu$ a finite real number.

## Proof

1.1 Each numerator is finite by [F3], and each denominator $h_j$ is finite and strictly positive by [F1]–[F2]. Thus every coefficient in the displayed finite sum is a defined real number. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Orthogonality of the $p_j$ gives, for each $i\le N$, $\int (u-\Pi_Nu)p_i\,d\mu =\int u p_i\,d\mu-\sum_{j=0}^{N}\frac{\int u p_j\,d\mu}{h_j}\int p_jp_i\,d\mu =0,$ because all terms with $j\ne i$ vanish and the $j=i$ term equals $\int u p_i\,d\mu$. Thus $\Pi_Nu\in V_N(\mu)$ has the required residual orthogonality. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $v\in V_N(\mu)$ has the same residual property, then $w=v-\Pi_Nu$ lies in $V_N(\mu)$ and is orthogonal to every basis vector, hence to itself. Positive definiteness in [F2] gives $\int w^2\,d\mu=0$, so $w=0$ in $L^2(\mu)$ and $v=\Pi_Nu$. This proves uniqueness. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $N\ge0$, take moment data of order $2N+1$ for a finite positive measure $\mu$ with support containing at least $N+2$ points, and use its $(N+1)$-node Gaussian rule and orthogonal polynomials $p_0,\ldots,p_N$. The matrix from [[alg-gaussian-orthogonal-polynomial-galerkin-mass-matrix]] has entries
$$M_{ij}^{G}=\int p_i(x)p_j(x)\,d\mu(x)= \begin{cases} 0,&i\ne j,\\ h_i,&i=j. \end{cases}$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $N\ge0$, moment data of order $2N+1$, its $(N+1)$-node Gaussian rule, and the corresponding orthogonal polynomials.

[F1] [[thm-gauss-rule-exact-through-degree-2m-minus-1-and-positive-weights]]: for an $m$-node rule from moment data of order $2m-1$, every polynomial of degree at most $2m-1$ integrates exactly.

[F2] [[def-weighted-orthogonal-polynomial-galerkin-space]]: $p_i$ is the monic degree-$i$ polynomial orthogonal to every lower-degree polynomial, and $h_i=\int p_i^2\,d\mu$.

[F3] [[alg-gaussian-orthogonal-polynomial-galerkin-mass-matrix]]: $M_{ij}^{G}$ is the Gaussian sum of $p_i p_j$ over the $N+1$ nodes.

## Proof
1.1 The product $p_i p_j$ has degree $i+j\le2N<2N+1=2(N+1)-1$. Thus [F1] applies with $m=N+1$ and gives $M_{ij}^{G}=\sum_{r=1}^{N+1}w_rp_i(\xi_r)p_j(\xi_r)=\int p_i(x)p_j(x)\,d\mu(x)$ by [F3]. [given, F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 If $i\ne j$, the higher-degree polynomial is orthogonal to the lower-degree one by [F2], so the integral in step 1.1 is zero. If $i=j$, it is $h_i$ by [F2]. This is the displayed diagonal matrix identity. [F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For $m,n\ge0$, the polynomials of [[def-legendre-polynomial-family-and-l2-pairing]] satisfy
$$\int_{-1}^1P_n(x)P_m(x)\,dx=\frac{2}{2n+1}\,\delta_{mn}, \qquad \int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)P_n'(x)P_m'(x)\,dx=\frac{2n(n+1)}{2n+1}\,\delta_{mn},$$
where $\delta_{mn}=1$ if $m=n$ and $0$ otherwise. Each $P_n$ has degree $n$ and nonzero leading coefficient, so $P_0,\ldots,P_N$ form a basis of polynomials of degree at most $N$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Nonnegative integers $m,n$ and the Rodrigues polynomials $P_k$.

[F1] [[def-legendre-polynomial-family-and-l2-pairing]]: $P_n=(2^nn!)^{-1}D^n(x^2-1)^n$ and $\langle p,q\rangle_L=\int_{-1}^1pq$.

[F2] [[thm-integration-by-parts]]: for differentiable factors with integrable derivatives on a closed interval, $\int uv'=[uv]-\int u'v$.

[F3] [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]]: $D(x^k)=kx^{k-1}$ for positive integer $k$, and constants differentiate to zero; repeated application gives the derivatives of monomials.

[F4] [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]: polynomial sums, products, and scalar multiples obey the usual derivative rules.

## Proof

1.1 Write $(x^2-1)^n=(x-1)^n(x+1)^n$. For every $j<n$, its $j$th derivative vanishes at both endpoints: by the product rule, every term differentiates each factor at most $j<n$ times and retains a positive power of the factor that vanishes at that endpoint. Thus $n$ integrations by parts in [F2] give, for every polynomial $q$ of degree less than $n$, $\int_{-1}^1P_nq=\frac{(-1)^n}{2^nn!}\int_{-1}^1(x^2-1)^nq^{(n)}=0,$ because $q^{(n)}=0$ by [F3]. Hence $P_n$ is orthogonal to every lower-degree polynomial. [F1, F2, F3, F4, given, induction]

2.1 The leading term of $(x^2-1)^n$ is $x^{2n}$; differentiating it $n$ times gives $(2n)!/n!$ times $x^n$ by [F3]. All other terms have lower degree after differentiation. Therefore $P_n$ has degree $n$ and leading coefficient $\kappa_n=(2n)!/(2^n(n!)^2)>0$. The distinct degrees imply the family $P_0,\ldots,P_N$ is linearly independent and spans every polynomial of degree at most $N$, by successive elimination of leading terms. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Since $P_n-\kappa_nx^n$ has degree less than $n$, step 1.1 gives $\int_{-1}^1P_n^2=\kappa_n\int_{-1}^1P_nx^n.$ Apply [F2] $n$ times to the Rodrigues formula against $x^n$. The endpoint terms vanish as in step 1.1 and $(x^n)^{(n)}=n!$, so $\int_{-1}^1P_nx^n=\frac1{2^n}\int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)^n\,dx.$ [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Put $J_n=\int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)^n dx$. Then $J_0=2$. For $n\ge1$, the endpoint values of $x(1-x^2)^n$ are zero, so integrating its derivative gives $0=J_n-2n(J_{n-1}-J_n),\qquad J_n=\frac{2n}{2n+1}J_{n-1}.$ Induction yields $J_n=2^{2n+1}(n!)^2/(2n+1)!$. Substituting this and $\kappa_n$ from step 2.1 into step 3.1 gives $\int P_n^2=2/(2n+1)$. Together with step 1.1 this proves the first orthogonality formula, including $n=0$. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, induction, algebra]

5.1 When $n=0$, $P_0=1$ and $Q_0=-((1-x^2)P_0')'=0$, so $Q_0=0\cdot P_0$. Now take $n\ge1$ and define $Q_n=-((1-x^2)P_n')'$. Its leading term is $n(n+1)\kappa_nx^n$, so $Q_n-n(n+1)P_n$ has degree less than $n$. For any polynomial $q$ of degree less than $n$, two integrations by parts give $\int_{-1}^1Q_nq=\int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)P_n'q'=-\int_{-1}^1P_n((1-x^2)q')'=0,$ where both boundary terms vanish because of the factor $1-x^2$, and the last polynomial paired with $P_n$ has degree less than $n$, so step 1.1 applies. Therefore $Q_n-n(n+1)P_n$ is a lower-degree polynomial orthogonal to every lower-degree polynomial. Expand it in the basis from step 2.1; the first formula and the positive norms in step 4.1 force every coefficient to be zero. Thus $Q_n=n(n+1)P_n$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 One integration by parts and step 5.1 give $\int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)P_n'P_m'=\int_{-1}^1Q_nP_m=n(n+1)\int_{-1}^1P_nP_m.$ The first formula, already proved in step 4.1 and step 1.1, yields the displayed weighted derivative identity for every $m,n\ge0$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $s\ge0$, $N\ge0$, and $u=\sum_{n\ge0}c_nP_n\in H_L^s$ from [[def-legendre-weighted-sobolev-scale]]. Then
$$
\|u-\Pi_Nu\|_{L_L^2}\le(1+(N+1)(N+2))^{-s/2}\|u\|_{H_L^s}.
$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A real $s\ge0$, an integer $N\ge0$, and a coefficient sequence in $H_L^s$.

[F1] [[def-legendre-weighted-sobolev-scale]]: $\Pi_Nu=\sum_{n=0}^Nc_nP_n$ and the $H_L^s$ coefficient weight is $(1+n(n+1))^s2/(2n+1)$.

[F2] [[lem-legendre-weighted-derivative-orthogonality-and-norm]]: $\int_{-1}^1P_nP_m=2\delta_{mn}/(2n+1)$.

## Proof
1.1 For a finite Legendre sum, [F1] gives $u-\Pi_Nu=\sum_{n>N}c_nP_n$. Orthogonality [F2] therefore gives $\|u-\Pi_Nu\|_{L_L^2}^2=\sum_{n>N}\frac{2}{2n+1}|c_n|^2.$ For every $n>N$, $1+n(n+1)\ge1+(N+1)(N+2)$; multiplying each term by the inverse weight gives the stated squared bound for finite sums. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Finite sums are dense in the completion defining $H_L^s$. The truncation $\Pi_N$ is contractive in both the coefficient norm and the $s=0$ norm, so the finite-sum inequality passes to the limit along any Cauchy sequence of finite sums. Taking square roots proves the claimed estimate for every $u\in H_L^s$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

For a continuous $f$ on $[-1,1]$, define its Chebyshev coefficients by
$$a_0(f)=\frac1\pi\int_0^\pi f(\cos\theta)\,d\theta,\qquad a_n(f)=\frac2\pi\int_0^\pi f(\cos\theta)\cos(n\theta)\,d\theta\quad(n\ge1).$$
For the analytic function $f_a(x)=1/(2-x)$, these coefficients are $a_0=1/\sqrt3$ and $a_n=2(2-\sqrt3)^n/\sqrt3$ for $n\ge1$, a geometric decay. For the nonsmooth function $f_s(x)=|x|$, they are $a_0=2/\pi$, $a_{2m}=4(-1)^{m-1}/(\pi(4m^2-1))$ for $m\ge1$, and $a_{2m+1}=0$; the nonzero coefficients decay algebraically like $m^{-2}$.

**Given:** The coefficient convention above and the two functions $f_a$ and $f_s$.

[F1] [[def-chebyshev-polynomials-first-and-second-kind]] and [[thm-chebyshev-multiple-angle-identities]]: $T_n(\cos\theta)=\cos(n\theta)$.

[F2] [[def-chebyshev-arcsine-weighted-l2-pairing]] and [[lem-chebyshev-polynomials-orthogonal-in-arcsine-weight]]: $\langle T_0,T_0\rangle_C=\pi$, $\langle T_n,T_n\rangle_C=\pi/2$ for $n\ge1$, and distinct modes are orthogonal.

[F3] [[lem-geometric-sequence-null]]: $q^{m+1}\to0$ for a real $q$ with $0<q<1$; [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]] gives complex modulus multiplicativity and the triangle inequality.

[F4] [[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]: a complex function is holomorphic on an open set when it is complex differentiable at every point there; [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]] supplies the complex field operations.

[F5] [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]]: $2\cos u\cos v=\cos(u+v)+\cos(u-v)$.

[F6] [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]] and [[thm-ftc-second-part]]: cosine has antiderivative $\sin(k\theta)/k$ for every nonzero integer $k$.

[F7] [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]] and [[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]]: $\sin(k\pi)=0$, $\sin((2m+1)\pi/2)=(-1)^m$, $\cos(k\pi)=(-1)^k$, and cosine is nonnegative on $[0,\pi/2]$ and nonpositive on $[\pi/2,\pi]$.

[F8] [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]: $e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$ and $|e^{i\theta}|=1$ for real $\theta$.

[F9] [[thm-sine-and-cosine-subtraction-formulas]]: $\cos(u-v)=\cos u\cos v+\sin u\sin v$.

[F10] [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]]: $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$.

[F12] [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]] and [[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]]: continuous functions on a compact interval are Riemann integrable, and finite linear combinations may be integrated termwise.

[F13] [[lem-uniform-integral-error-bound]]: integrable functions uniformly within $\eta$ on $[0,\pi]$ have integrals differing by at most $\pi\eta$.

The subtraction identity [F9] gives $\cos(n(\pi-\theta))=(-1)^n\cos(n\theta)$, so reflection makes each odd coefficient integral its own negative. ## Definition

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $c:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be smooth (that is, $C^\infty$) with $1\le m<d$, let $M$ be a constant symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix, and let $V:U\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. A **holonomic constraint** is the position condition $c(q)=0$. Write $J(q)=Dc(q)$, let $Q=\{q\in U:c(q)=0\}$, and define its regular part by $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}=\{q\in Q:\operatorname{rank}J(q)=m\}$. For $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $A(q)=J(q)M^{-1}J(q)^T$ is positive definite. On a compact regular chart $K\subset Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $A^{-1}$ is uniformly bounded: $\sup_{q\in K}\|A(q)^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\infty$.

A position-momentum pair $(q,p)$ is **consistent** when $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and $J(q)M^{-1}p=0$. The **regular constrained phase manifold** is
$$\mathcal M=\{(q,p)\in U\times\mathbb R^d:c(q)=0,\ J(q)M^{-1}p=0,\ q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}\}.$$
The ambient canonical two-form is $\omega_0=\sum_{i=1}^d dq_i\wedge dp_i$; its restriction to $\mathcal M$ is denoted $\omega_{\mathcal M}$.

For $v=M^{-1}p$, the constrained Hamilton equations are
$$\dot q=v,\qquad \dot p=-\nabla V(q)-J(q)^T\lambda,$$
with multiplier
$$\lambda=A(q)^{-1}\bigl(D^2c(q)[v,v]-J(q)M^{-1}\nabla V(q)\bigr).$$
Here $D^2c(q)[v,v]\in\mathbb R^m$ has components $v^TD^2c_j(q)v$. This multiplier is the one that keeps both $c(q)=0$ and $J(q)M^{-1}p=0$ satisfied.

## Statement

Let $P\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $r\in\{1,2\}$ and $k\ge1$, and let $f:(-\delta,\delta)\times P\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^{k+r}$. Suppose $\partial_h^j f(0,\alpha)=0$ for every $\alpha\in P$ and $0\le j<r$. Then $f(h,\alpha)/h^r$, initially defined for $h\ne0$, has a $C^k$ extension $F$ to $(-\delta,\delta)\times P$. Its mixed derivatives at zero satisfy
$$\partial_h^\ell\partial_\alpha^\beta F(0,\alpha)=\frac{\ell!}{(r+\ell)!}\partial_h^{r+\ell}\partial_\alpha^\beta f(0,\alpha)\qquad(\ell+|\beta|\le k).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

[F1] [[thm-multivariable-taylor-formula-with-lagrange-remainder]]: a $C^{s+1}$ map on a convex neighborhood has its degree-$s$ Taylor polynomial with a remainder of order $s+1$ along each line.

[F2] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: differentiating a composition with a coordinate line gives the corresponding directional derivative.

[F3] [[thm-mean-value-inequality-for-total-derivatives]]: on a convex interval, a derivative bound gives the corresponding scalar increment bound.

## Proof

1.1 For each parameter multi-index $\beta$, differentiate the identities $\partial_h^j f(0,\alpha)=0$ in $\alpha$ using [F2]; thus every $\partial_\alpha^\beta f$ also vanishes to order $r$ in $h$ at zero. [given, F2]

2.1 For each parameter multi-index $\beta$ with $|\beta|\le k$, put $k_\beta=k-|\beta|$, $N=r+k_\beta$, and $g_\beta(h)=\partial_\alpha^\beta f(h,\alpha)$. For every $s\le k_\beta$, put $m=N-s$. If $m\ge2$, apply [F1] componentwise to $g_\beta^{(s)}$ through degree $m-1$; continuity of its highest derivative lets us replace the Lagrange coefficient at $\theta h$ by its value at zero plus $o(1)$. If $m=1$, subtract the linear Taylor polynomial: the derivative of the remainder is $o(1)$ by continuity, so [F3] gives a remainder $o(|h|)$. Thus in every case $g_\beta^{(s)}(h)$ equals its Taylor polynomial through degree $m$ plus $o(|h|^m)$. By step 1.1 all coefficients of degrees below $r$ vanish. For $h\ne0$, the quotient rule expresses the $\ell$th derivative of $g_\beta/h^r$ as a finite linear combination of $h^{-r-\ell+s}g_\beta^{(s)}(h)$, $0\le s\le\ell$. Substituting the expansions shows that the remainder terms are $o(|h|^{k_\beta-\ell})$; the polynomial part has a continuous extension whose $\ell$th derivative at zero is $\ell!\partial_h^{r+\ell}\partial_\alpha^\beta f(0,\alpha)/(r+\ell)!$. Continuity of the derivatives on compact parameter neighborhoods makes these limits locally uniform in $\alpha$. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Define the value at $h=0$ by the displayed limit formula. For each $|\beta|+\ell\le k$, step 2.1 gives a locally uniform limit for the corresponding derivative as $h\to0$; at $h=0$ these formulas are differentiable in $\alpha$ because $f$ is $C^{k+r}$, and their $h$-derivatives agree with the next displayed coefficient. Induction on total derivative order therefore shows that all mixed partial derivatives through order $k$ exist and are continuous across $h=0$. The extension is $C^k$ with the asserted formula. [step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Under the hypotheses of [[def-regular-holonomic-phase-space-and-dynamics]], let $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}=\{q\in Q:\operatorname{rank}J(q)=m\}$. It is a smooth manifold of dimension $d-m$. Choose a local configuration chart $\phi:O\subseteq\mathbb R^{d-m}\to Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and write $T=D\phi$, $G=T^TMT$. The cotangent coordinates $\pi=T^Tp$ identify the part of $\mathcal M$ over this chart locally with $T^*Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$: the unique consistent ambient momentum representing $\pi$ is $p=MTG^{-1}\pi$. In these coordinates the restricted canonical one-form $p^Tdq$ is $\pi^Tdx$, so the restricted two-form is $\omega_{\mathcal M}=\sum_{j=1}^{d-m}dx_j\wedge d\pi_j$. It is closed and nondegenerate, hence is symplectic on the regular phase manifold.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The objects and regularity hypotheses in [[def-regular-holonomic-phase-space-and-dynamics]], and the canonical symplectic convention in [[def-symplectic-form-and-symplectic-manifold]].

[F1] [[def-regular-holonomic-phase-space-and-dynamics]]: $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}=\{q\in Q:\operatorname{rank}J(q)=m\}$, $M$ is constant SPD, and $\mathcal M$ consists of $(q,p)$ with $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and $JM^{-1}p=0$.

[F2] [[thm-parametrized-implicit-function-theorem-with-higher-regularity]]: if a square block derivative of a $C^k$ map is invertible at a zero, its zero set is locally the graph of a unique $C^k$ function; this applies for every finite $k$ when the map is smooth.

[F3] [[def-symplectic-form-and-symplectic-manifold]]: a symplectic form is a smooth closed two-form that is pointwise nondegenerate.

[F4] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: the derivative of a composite is the composite of its derivatives.

## Proof

1.1 At any $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, full row rank of $J(q)$ gives a permutation of coordinates $q=(x,y)$ for which the $m\times m$ block $D_yc(q)$ is invertible. Apply [F2] to the smooth map $c$ for each finite $k\ge1$. The resulting local graphs agree with the unique $C^1$ graph on overlaps, so that graph is $C^k$ locally for every $k$ and hence smooth. Thus locally $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is $y=\psi(x)$; $\phi(x)=(x,\psi(x))$ parametrizes it, and $D\phi$ has rank $d-m$ with image $\ker J$. [F1, F2, construct]

2.1 Define $G(x)=D\phi(x)^TMD\phi(x)$. For every nonzero $\xi$, $D\phi\,\xi\ne0$ and $\xi^TG(x)\xi=(D\phi\,\xi)^TM(D\phi\,\xi)>0$, so $G$ is invertible. Its entries are smooth, and $G^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}(G)/\det G$ is smooth because $\det G>0$. For a cotangent coordinate $\pi\in\mathbb R^{d-m}$, put $p=MD\phi\,G^{-1}\pi$. Then $JM^{-1}p=JD\phi\,G^{-1}\pi=0$ and $D\phi^Tp=G G^{-1}\pi=\pi$. Conversely, if $JM^{-1}p=0$, then $M^{-1}p=D\phi\,\xi$ for a unique $\xi$, and $D\phi^Tp=G\xi$; hence the displayed formula gives the unique ambient $p$ representing $\pi$. Both this map and its inverse $(q,p)\mapsto(x,D\phi(x)^Tp)$ are smooth, so $(x,\pi)\mapsto(\phi(x),p)$ is a local diffeomorphism from $T^*Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ onto the part of $\mathcal M$ over this chart. [step 1.1, F1, algebra]

3.1 Let $\theta_0=p^Tdq$ be the ambient canonical one-form. Under the chart just constructed, $dq=D\phi\,dx$ and $D\phi^Tp=\pi$, so its pullback is $\pi^Tdx$. Therefore the pullback of $\omega_0=-d\theta_0$ is $\sum_{j=1}^{d-m}dx_j\wedge d\pi_j$, which is closed and nondegenerate. [F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Every point of $\mathcal M$ has a chart of this form; the local calculation proves the restricted two-form is closed and nondegenerate everywhere. By [F3] it is symplectic, as claimed. [F3, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

Fix a compact regular configuration chart from [[def-regular-holonomic-phase-space-and-dynamics]] and a compact momentum set. Use the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^{2d}$ for phase-state differences. Each point of its consistent phase set has a neighborhood $U_j$ with a smooth retraction $\Pi_j:U_j\to\mathcal M$ such that $\Pi_j$ is the identity on $U_j\cap\mathcal M$ and
$$\|\Pi_j(q,p)-(q,p)\|\le C_j\bigl(\|c(q)\|_2+\|J(q)M^{-1}p\|_2\bigr).$$
A finite number of these neighborhoods cover the compact phase set, so one constant works for all of them. In particular, residuals of sizes $O(h^4)$ and $O(h^3)$ admit a consistent restoration at distance $O(h^3)$, uniformly on the chart.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A compact regular chart, compact momentum set, and the smooth full-row-rank constraint data in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-regular-holonomic-phase-space-and-dynamics]]: $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}=\{q\in Q:\operatorname{rank}J(q)=m\}$, $A=JM^{-1}J^T$ is uniformly invertible on the compact chart, and $(q,p)\in\mathcal M$ means $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and $JM^{-1}p=0$.

[F2] [[thm-parametrized-implicit-function-theorem-with-higher-regularity]]: an invertible square derivative block gives a unique local $C^k$ graph for a $C^k$ zero-set equation; since $c$ is smooth, its local graph is smooth.

[F3] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: derivatives of a composite are obtained by composing the derivatives.

[F4] [[thm-mean-value-inequality-for-total-derivatives]]: a uniform derivative bound on a convex neighborhood gives the corresponding Lipschitz bound.

## Proof

1.1 At a point of the compact regular chart $K\subset Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, permute coordinates as $q=(x,y)$ so $D_yc$ is an invertible $m\times m$ block. Apply [F2] for each finite regularity order; uniqueness makes these graphs agree locally, so the graph $y=\psi(x)$ is smooth. Write $\phi(x)=(x,\psi(x))$ and $T(x)=D\phi(x)$. Since $J(\phi(x))T(x)=0$ and both kernels have dimension $d-m$, $\operatorname{im}T=\ker J$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 After shrinking to a convex coordinate neighborhood, $B(x)=D_yc(x,\psi(x))$ remains invertible and $\|B(x)^{-1}(D_yc(x,y)-B(x))\|\le\frac12$. Set $R_x(y)=c(x,y)-B(x)(y-\psi(x))$. Then $R_x(\psi(x))=0$ and the derivative of $B(x)^{-1}R_x$ has norm at most $\frac12$. The mean-value inequality [F4] gives $\|B(x)^{-1}R_x(y)\|\le\frac12\|y-\psi(x)\|$. Since $B^{-1}c=(y-\psi)+B^{-1}R_x(y)$, it follows that $\|q-\phi(x)\|=\|y-\psi(x)\|\le 2\|B(x)^{-1}\|\,\|c(q)\|$. Compactness makes the constant uniform on a finite chart cover. [F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For $\bar q=\phi(x)$, put $G=T^TMT$ and define $\bar p=MTG^{-1}T^Tp$. Positive definiteness of $M$ and injectivity of $T$ make $G$ invertible; its smooth entries and positive determinant give a smooth inverse by $G^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}(G)/\det G$. Then $J(\bar q)M^{-1}\bar p=0$ and $T^T(p-\bar p)=0$. Since $\ker T^T$ and $\operatorname{im}J(\bar q)^T$ both have dimension $m$ and the latter is contained in the former, $p-\bar p=J(\bar q)^T\eta$ for a unique $\eta$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The identity $J(\bar q)M^{-1}(p-\bar p)=A(\bar q)\eta$ and [F1] imply $\|p-\bar p\|\le C\|A(\bar q)^{-1}\|\bigl(\|J(q)M^{-1}p\|+\|J(\bar q)-J(q)\|\,\|M^{-1}p\|\bigr)$. The momentum set is bounded and $J$ is locally Lipschitz, so step 2.1 bounds the right side by $C(\|J(q)M^{-1}p\|+\|c(q)\|)$. Thus $\Pi(q,p)=(\bar q,\bar p)$ has the asserted distance bound and lies in $\mathcal M$. If $(q,p)\in\mathcal M$, then $\bar q=q$ and the formula for $\bar p$ returns $p$, so $\Pi$ is the identity there. By [F3] the coordinate formula is smooth, and it is the identity on the consistent phase set in this neighborhood. Shrink the finitely many neighborhoods so their closures lie in an open regular set; continuity keeps $A^{-1}$ and the required derivatives uniformly bounded there. A finite subcover gives finitely many such local retractions and a uniform constant. [F1, F3, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Use the data of [[def-regular-holonomic-phase-space-and-dynamics]]. For a consistent input $(q,p)\in\mathcal M$, put $v=M^{-1}p$ and
$$\lambda_* =\mu_* =\frac12A(q)^{-1}\bigl(D^2c(q)[v,v]-J(q)M^{-1}\nabla V(q)\bigr).$$
For nonzero signed $h$, form the sequential scaled residual equations
$$F_q(\lambda)=h^{-2}c\!\left(q+hM^{-1}\left(p-\frac h2\nabla V(q)-hJ(q)^T\lambda\right)\right)=0,$$
$$F_p(\mu;\lambda)=h^{-1}J(q_1)M^{-1}p_1=0,$$
where $q_1,p_{1/2},p_1$ are given by the updates below. The selected multiplier pair, when it exists uniquely, is the local root branch whose limits as $h\to0$ are $\lambda_*$ and $\mu_*$. This defines a partial exact step map; no root-existence assertion is part of this definition.

For such a selected pair $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb R^m$, define
$$p_{1/2}=p-\frac h2\nabla V(q)-hJ(q)^T\lambda,\qquad q_1=q+hM^{-1}p_{1/2},$$
$$p_1=p_{1/2}-\frac h2\nabla V(q_1)-hJ(q_1)^T\mu.$$
The position and momentum equations are respectively $c(q_1)=0$ and $J(q_1)M^{-1}p_1=0$. At $h=0$ define the step to be the identity.

Here $\lambda,\mu$ are force-level multipliers: the corresponding constraint impulses are $hJ^T\lambda$ and $hJ^T\mu$. This scaling keeps the limiting multiplier equations nonsingular as $h\to0$. The position equation is SHAKE; the final momentum equation is the RATTLE tangency correction.

**Given:** A compact regular chart, a consistent initial pair $(q_0,p_0)$, and the constrained equations in the Statement.

A finite cover of $C$ therefore gives a common $h_0(C)>0$ for $|h|<h_0(C)$; the derivatives of each fixed finite order are uniformly bounded on this cover, and the two multiplier Jacobians remain uniformly invertible there. ## Statement

Let $C\subset\mathcal M$ be compact and choose a compact phase-space neighborhood $\overline C$ of $C$ contained in a regular coordinate chart. There is $h_0(\overline C)>0$ such that for $|h|<h_0(\overline C)$ the exact map $\Psi_h$ of [[def-regular-classical-rattle-step-map]] is defined near $C$, its image lies in $\overline C$, and its reverse branch is defined near that image; the reverse branch is a local inverse, so $\Psi_h$ is a local diffeomorphism near $C$. On this neighborhood it preserves $\omega_{\mathcal M}$:
$$\Psi_h^*\omega_{\mathcal M}=\omega_{\mathcal M}.$$
Here symplecticity of a map means that it is a local diffeomorphism whose pullback preserves the two-form; the form itself is symplectic in the sense of [[def-symplectic-form-and-symplectic-manifold]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The compact phase-space neighborhood in the Statement, the exact selected RATTLE map, and the symplectic cotangent coordinates.

[F1] [[def-regular-holonomic-phase-space-and-dynamics]]: on the regular phase manifold $\mathcal M$, $\omega_{\mathcal M}$ is the restriction of the ambient canonical form $\omega_0=\sum dq_i\wedge dp_i$.

[F2] [[lem-regular-holonomic-phase-space-is-symplectic-cotangent]]: in local configuration coordinates $x$, a consistent ambient momentum represents a cotangent covector $\pi=D\phi(x)^Tp$ and $\omega_{\mathcal M}=\sum dx_i\wedge d\pi_i$.

[F3] [[def-regular-classical-rattle-step-map]]: RATTLE uses the two half-force updates, the constrained drift $q_1-q=hM^{-1}p_{1/2}$, and normal constraint impulses at $q$ and $q_1$.

[F4] [[lem-rattle-scaled-position-and-momentum-branches]]: the selected branches define a smooth local map, with a common step range on each compact phase subset.

[F5] [[def-symplectic-form-and-symplectic-manifold]]: a symplectic form is a smooth closed two-form that is pointwise nondegenerate.

[F6] [[thm-rattle-exact-constraint-preservation-and-reversibility]]: the signed-step map has inverse $\Psi_{-h}$ on the selected regular branches.

1.1 If $h=0$, then $\Psi_0$ is the identity and preserves $\omega_{\mathcal M}$. Assume $h\ne0$. On a local configuration chart define $L_h(q,q_1)=\frac{1}{2h}(q_1-q)^TM(q_1-q)-\frac h2(V(q)+V(q_1))$. Differentiating gives $-D_1L_h=p_{1/2}+\frac h2\nabla V(q)$ and $D_2L_h=p_{1/2}-\frac h2\nabla V(q_1)$. By [F3], the first expression differs from $p$ by the normal vector $-hJ(q)^T\lambda$, and the second differs from $p_1$ by $hJ(q_1)^T\mu$. Each normal vector vanishes on tangent variations of $Q$, so the restricted cotangent covectors satisfy $p|_{T_qQ}=-D_1L_h|_{T_qQ}$ and $p_1|_{T_{q_1}Q}=D_2L_h|_{T_{q_1}Q}$. [F3, given, algebra]

2.1 Let $\theta$ be the canonical one-form on $T^*Q$, $\theta_{(q,\pi)}(\delta q,\delta\pi)=\pi(\delta q)$. The identities in step 1.1 give $\Psi_h^*\theta-\theta=d(L_h(q,q_1(q,p)))$ on the input chart, because both sides applied to an input variation equal $D_1L_h\,\delta q+D_2L_h\,\delta q_1$. Hence this is $\Psi_h^*\omega_{\mathcal M}=\omega_{\mathcal M}$. The branch map is smooth by [F4] and locally invertible by [F6]. By [F2] and [F5], the preserved form is the symplectic form on $\mathcal M$; this proves the stated symplecticity. [F1, F2, F4, F5, F6, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

For finite budgets $N_q,N_p$, the algorithm [[alg-finite-budget-rattle-step-with-scaled-residuals]] terminates after two finite residual-solver calls at most and returns one of its stated success or failure statuses. This is a termination claim only; it does not assert the residual tolerances will be met.

**Given:** Finite nonnegative budgets $N_q,N_p$, a consistent input, and the algorithm in the Statement; for nonzero $h$, also its supplied open branch balls, $C^1$ residual maps defined on those balls, returning evaluation/arithmetic/norm/domain-test primitives, and terminating exact factorization and retained-factor solve backends.

Every failure status and returned last valid iterate is specified by the procedure.

[F2] [[alg-newton-chord-implicit-residual-with-factorization-reuse]]: chord mode enters successive indices $k=0,\ldots,N$. At each index it evaluates the residual and tests its norm; it returns `root` when the tolerance is met, and at $k=N$ otherwise returns `iteration-budget-exhausted` before another correction. At a continuing index it refreshes on schedule, returns `singular-jacobian` for a singular factorization, obtains a correction from the retained factor solve, returns `invalid-trial` if the trial leaves the open domain, and otherwise advances to $k+1$. At index $k$, its residual evaluation and norm comparison terminate by the admitted primitive contract. The tolerance and budget branches return the current valid iterate and its actual residual norm. If neither branch returns, then $k<N$; one terminating Jacobian evaluation and factorization attempt either return `singular-jacobian` with this same data or supply a retained factor. Its terminating exact solve produces the correction. The returning domain test either returns `invalid-trial` with the old valid iterate and evaluated residual or admits the new iterate and increments the index. Thus induction preserves domain membership and validity of all returned residual data. [F1, F2, given, induction]

2.1 Every continuing pass strictly increments $k$, and an entered pass $k=N$ returns before a factorization or correction. Consequently there are at most $N+1$ residual checks and at most $N$ correction attempts, Jacobian assemblies, factorization attempts, and retained-factor solves. Each pass consists of finitely many returning operations by step 1.1, so the call terminates, including when $N=0$. These are counts of loop operations, not a uniform bound on the internal cost of a supplied evaluation or backend. [F2, step 1.1, induction]

## Statement

Let $\mathcal C$ be a compact subset of the regular phase manifold, contained in a convex phase-coordinate chart whose closure lies inside a regular chart. Let $(q,p)\in\mathcal C$, let $(q_1,p_1)$ be its exact RATTLE step, and let $(\widetilde q_1,\widetilde p_1)$ be a successful output of [[alg-finite-budget-rattle-step-with-scaled-residuals]] whose multiplier iterates remain in the chosen convex branch balls over $\mathcal C$. Define
$$\varepsilon_q=\|h^{-2}c(\widetilde q_1)\|_2,\qquad \varepsilon_p=\|h^{-1}J(\widetilde q_1)M^{-1}\widetilde p_1\|_2.$$
For sufficiently small $0<|h|$, there is a constant $C$ uniform over $\mathcal C$ such that
$$\|\widetilde q_1-q_1\|\le Ch^2\varepsilon_q,\qquad \|\widetilde p_1-p_1\|\le C|h|(\varepsilon_q+\varepsilon_p).$$
For the repeated-trajectory claim, choose compact phase tubes $\mathcal C_0\subset\operatorname{relint}(\mathcal C_1)$ in such a chart, with the coordinate image of $\mathcal C_1$ contained in a convex coordinate neighborhood with compact closure inside the regular chart. Suppose the exact-solve RATTLE iterates from a common initial state in $\mathcal C_0$ remain in $\mathcal C_0$ on the fixed-time grids under consideration. Restore each successful finite-solve output using a local retraction from [[lem-regular-holonomic-phase-residuals-control-distance-to-phase-manifold]] before using it as the next input. If both scaled residuals are bounded by a fixed sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ at each step, then for sufficiently small $h$ the restored trajectory remains in $\mathcal C_1$ and differs from the exact-solve RATTLE trajectory by $O(\varepsilon)$ uniformly on the grid. If instead both residuals are at most $C_0h^2$, the difference is $O(h^2)$, and the unscaled position and tangency residuals of each unprojected solver output are respectively $O(h^4)$ and $O(h^3)$. The finite solver's raw output need not be consistent, so the global estimate is for the restored trajectory.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A compact phase subset $\mathcal C$, a consistent input $(q,p)\in\mathcal C$, exact and approximate multiplier iterates in the selected branch neighborhoods over $\mathcal C$, and the scaled residuals in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-regular-classical-rattle-step-map]]: the exact updates use the impulses $hJ(q)^T\lambda$, $hJ(q_1)^T\mu$, and impose $c(q_1)=0$, $J(q_1)M^{-1}p_1=0$.

[F2] [[lem-rattle-scaled-position-and-momentum-branches]]: the scaled equations have unique smooth local roots, with a common step range and uniform derivative and inverse-Jacobian bounds on each compact phase subset.

[F3] [[alg-finite-budget-rattle-step-with-scaled-residuals]]: on its success status the algorithm returns the state, both multiplier iterates, and the scaled residual norms $\varepsilon_q,\varepsilon_p$ defined above.

[F4] [[def-implicit-residual-and-algebraic-error-units]]: a residual norm is not a forward-error bound without a separate inverse or stability estimate.

[F5] [[thm-mean-value-inequality-for-total-derivatives]]: a uniform derivative bound on a convex neighborhood yields a uniform Lipschitz estimate.

[F6] [[lem-regular-holonomic-phase-residuals-control-distance-to-phase-manifold]]: finitely many local smooth retractions cover a compact regular phase set, and all satisfy the uniform bound $\|\Pi_j(q,p)-(q,p)\|\le C(\|c(q)\|_2+\|J(q)M^{-1}p\|_2)$ on their domains.

## Proof

1.1 For $F_q(\lambda)=h^{-2}c(q_1(\lambda))$, [F2] gives $D_\lambda F_q=-A(q)+o(1)$ uniformly on the branch ball. Shrink it so $\|A(q)^{-1}(D_\lambda F_q+A(q))\|\le\frac12$. The derivative of $G(\lambda)=A(q)^{-1}F_q(\lambda)+\lambda$ is then bounded by $1/2$. Since $F_q(\lambda)=0$ at the exact root $\lambda$, [F5] along the segment to $\widetilde\lambda$ gives $\|G(\widetilde\lambda)-G(\lambda)\|\le\frac12\|\widetilde\lambda-\lambda\|$. As $A^{-1}F_q(\widetilde\lambda)=G(\widetilde\lambda)-G(\lambda)-(\widetilde\lambda-\lambda)$, it follows that $\|\widetilde\lambda-\lambda\|\le2\|A(q)^{-1}\|\varepsilon_q$. This inverse estimate is needed because [F4] alone does not convert residual size to state error. [F2, F3, F4, F5, given, algebra]

2.1 The position formula gives $\widetilde q_1-q_1=-h^2M^{-1}J(q)^T(\widetilde\lambda-\lambda)$ and $\widetilde p_{1/2}-p_{1/2}=-hJ(q)^T(\widetilde\lambda-\lambda)$. The uniform matrix bounds and step 1.1 yield $\|\widetilde q_1-q_1\|\le Ch^2\varepsilon_q$ and $\|\widetilde p_{1/2}-p_{1/2}\|\le C|h|\varepsilon_q$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For fixed $\widetilde\lambda$, the final scaled tangency residual is affine in $\mu$ with derivative exactly $-A(\widetilde q_1)$. Uniform invertibility bounds the distance from $\widetilde\mu$ to the exact momentum root for this $\widetilde\lambda$ by $C\varepsilon_p$. The smooth momentum branch in [F2] changes that exact root by at most $C\varepsilon_q$ when $\widetilde\lambda$ replaces $\lambda$, using step 1.1 and the uniform branch derivative bound. [F2, F3, F5, step 1.1]

3.1 In the final momentum formula, the initial half-momentum difference contributes $O(|h|\varepsilon_q)$ by step 2.1; changing the position in the smooth force and constraint Jacobian contributes $O(|h|^3\varepsilon_q)$; changing the final multiplier contributes $O(|h|(\varepsilon_q+\varepsilon_p))$ by step 2.2. Their sum proves $\|\widetilde p_1-p_1\|\le C|h|(\varepsilon_q+\varepsilon_p)$ and hence the one-step estimates. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 The residual definitions give $\|c(\widetilde q_1)\|=|h|^2\varepsilon_q$ and $\|J(\widetilde q_1)M^{-1}\widetilde p_1\|=|h|\varepsilon_p$. Whenever the output lies in a neighborhood $U_j$ from [F6], its local retraction changes it by at most $C(|h|^2\varepsilon_q+|h|\varepsilon_p)\le C|h|(\varepsilon_q+\varepsilon_p)$ for $|h|\le1$. The compact branch bounds and $\Psi_0=\mathrm{id}$ imply $\Psi_h(\mathcal C_1)\subset D$ for sufficiently small $|h|$. Apply [F6] to $D$ and choose its finite retraction cover with a common distance constant. The union of these open domains contains the compact set $D$, hence contains some uniform ambient neighborhood of it. For every restored input in $\mathcal C_1$, step 3.1 puts its raw output within $O(|h|(\varepsilon_q+\varepsilon_p))$ of the exact step from that same input in $D$. Bounded scaled residuals and sufficiently small $|h|$ therefore place the raw output in this union. The same-input exact step need not belong to the reference tube $\mathcal C_0$. Thus the retraction is defined, and the restored update differs from the exact RATTLE update by at most $C|h|(\varepsilon_q+\varepsilon_p)$. [F1, F2, F3, F6, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Work in the phase coordinates of the Statement and choose a slightly larger compact convex coordinate neighborhood on which the branches and their first derivatives are bounded by [F2]. Since $\Psi_0$ is the identity, $D_z\Psi_h=I+O(h)$ uniformly there, so [F5] gives a Lipschitz factor $1+Lh$ for small positive $h$. The one-step estimate and the retraction bound, with equivalence of ambient and chart norms on the compact tube, bound each restored solver perturbation by $K h(\varepsilon_q+\varepsilon_p)$. Starting with the same initial state, the error therefore obeys $e_{n+1}\le(1+Lh)e_n+K h(\varepsilon_q+\varepsilon_p)$ until a first exit from $\mathcal C_1$. Iteration gives $e_n\le K_T\varepsilon$ for fixed residual bound and $e_n\le K_T h^2$ when each residual is at most $C_0h^2$. Choose $\varepsilon$ small enough, or $h$ small enough in the second case, that this bound is less than the positive coordinate distance from $\mathcal C_0$ to the boundary of $\mathcal C_1$; then no first exit occurs. Step 4.1, applied until this first-exit argument closes, places every raw output in a retraction neighborhood for small $h$. Finally, the unscaled residuals are exactly $h^2\varepsilon_q$ and $h\varepsilon_p$, hence $O(h^4)$ and $O(h^3)$ in the second case. [F2, F5, F6, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

For a planar pendulum of mass $m>0$ and rod length $\ell>0$, let $M=mI_2$, $V(q)=mgq_2$, and $c(q)=(\|q\|_2^2-\ell^2)/2$. If $c(q)=0$ and $q^Tp=0$, the multiplier in the constrained equations is
$$\lambda(q,p)=\frac{\|p\|_2^2/m-mgq_2}{\ell^2}.$$
At the bottom rest state $q=(0,-\ell)$, $p=0$, this gives $\lambda=mg/\ell$ and zero acceleration.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $M=mI_2$, the constraint and potential in the Example, and consistent data $c(q)=0$, $q^Tp=0$.

[F1] [[def-regular-holonomic-phase-space-and-dynamics]]: $A(q)=J(q)M^{-1}J(q)^T$ and $\lambda=A^{-1}(D^2c[v,v]-JM^{-1}\nabla V)$, where $v=M^{-1}p$.

[F2] [[thm-local-holonomic-constrained-hamiltonian-flow]]: these equations define the unique local constrained flow for consistent data in the regular chart.

## Verification

1.1 Here $J(q)=q^T$, $A(q)=q^Tq/m=\ell^2/m$, $D^2c[v,v]=\|p\|_2^2/m^2$, and $JM^{-1}\nabla V=gq_2$. Substitution into [F1] gives $\lambda=(\|p\|_2^2/m-mgq_2)/\ell^2$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 At $q=(0,-\ell)$ and $p=0$, the multiplier is $mg/\ell$. The acceleration is $\dot p=-mg(0,1)-\lambda(0,-\ell)=(0,0)$; moreover $c(q)=0$ and $q^Tp=0$, so this is a consistent equilibrium of the local flow [F2]. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let $M=mI_2$, $m,\ell,\omega>0$, $V=0$, and $c(q)=(\|q\|_2^2-\ell^2)/2$. Start from $q_0=(\ell,0)$ and $p_0=(0,m\omega\ell)$, and take $0<h\omega\le\frac12$. The selected exact RATTLE step has
$$q_1=\ell\bigl(\sqrt{1-h^2\omega^2},h\omega\bigr),\qquad p_1=m\omega\ell\bigl(-h\omega,\sqrt{1-h^2\omega^2}\bigr).$$
Its position constraint and momentum tangency are exact. The exact constrained flow rotates by angle $h\omega$, whereas RATTLE rotates by $\arcsin(h\omega)$, so the one-step phase defect is $O(h^3)$ as $h\omega\to0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $M=mI_2$, the circle constraint, the free-particle potential, initial data, and step range in the Example.

[F1] [[def-regular-holonomic-phase-space-and-dynamics]]: consistency is $c(q)=0$ and $q^TM^{-1}p=0$.

[F2] [[def-regular-classical-rattle-step-map]]: the exact position and momentum updates use the two force-level multipliers and impose $c(q_1)=0$ and $q_1^TM^{-1}p_1=0$.

[F3] [[thm-local-holonomic-constrained-hamiltonian-flow]]: consistent data evolve by $\dot q=M^{-1}p$ and $\dot p=-\nabla V-J^T\lambda$.

[F4] [[thm-multivariable-taylor-formula-with-lagrange-remainder]]: a $C^3$ scalar function on a convex interval has its degree-two Taylor polynomial with a cubic Lagrange remainder.

## Verification

1.1 The initial data are consistent because $\|q_0\|_2=\ell$ and $q_0^Tp_0=0$. The position multiplier equation gives $q_1=q_0+\frac hm(p_0-h\lambda q_0)$; choosing $\lambda=m(1-\sqrt{1-h^2\omega^2})/h^2=m\omega^2/(1+\sqrt{1-h^2\omega^2})$ yields the stated $q_1$, whose squared norm is $\ell^2$. This multiplier tends to $m\omega^2/2$, the position branch center. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 With $\mu=\lambda$, the final RATTLE equation gives the stated $p_1$; $\mu$ has the same limit $m\omega^2/2$, so the unique local branch selects this root. Direct multiplication gives $q_1^Tp_1=0$ and $\|p_1\|_2=m\omega\ell$, so both exact constraints hold. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The continuous multiplier is $\lambda_c=m\omega^2$, hence the exact flow is $q(t)=\ell(\cos\omega t,\sin\omega t)$ and $p(t)=m\omega\ell(-\sin\omega t,\cos\omega t)$. ## Statement

Let $0=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_N=1$ be a finite interval partition, $h:=\max_j(x_{j+1}-x_j)$, and $u\in C^2([0,1])$. Let $I_hu$ be the continuous piecewise-linear function with nodal values $I_hu(x_j)=u(x_j)$. Then

$$\|(u-I_hu)'\|_{L^2(0,1)}\le h\|u''\|_{L^\infty(0,1)}.$$

If $u(0)=u(1)=0$, then $I_hu$ also vanishes at both endpoints.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite interval partition, $h$ its maximum cell length, and $u\in C^2([0,1])$.

[F1] [[thm-ftc-second-part]]: if a differentiable function has an integrable derivative, its increment is the integral of that derivative.

[F2] [[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]]: for an integrable function bounded in absolute value by $C$, the integral over an interval of length $\ell$ has absolute value at most $C\ell$.

[F3] For every nonnegative measurable $q$, the map $E\mapsto\int_E q$ is a measure, hence finitely additive on disjoint measurable cells ([[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]). Nonnegative Lebesgue integrals preserve bounds ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]); a constant bound integrates as that constant times the interval length ([[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]], [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]).

[F4] [[thm-extreme-value-r]]: a continuous function on the compact interval $[0,1]$ has a finite maximum and minimum.

## Proof

1.1 Fix a cell $K=[a,b]=[x_j,x_{j+1}]$ of length $h_K$. Its interpolant slope is $s_K=(u(b)-u(a))/h_K=h_K^{-1}\int_a^bu'(t)\,dt$ by [F1]. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 For every $x\in K$, $u'(x)-s_K=h_K^{-1}\int_a^b(u'(x)-u'(t))\,dt$. A second use of [F1] and then [F2] gives $|u'(x)-u'(t)|\le\|u''\|_\infty|x-t|\le h_K\|u''\|_\infty$, hence $|u'(x)-s_K|\le h_K\|u''\|_\infty$. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The continuous function $|u''|$ has a finite maximum by [F4]. On each open cell $K^\circ=(x_j,x_{j+1})$, $q=|u'-s_K|^2$ is continuous and hence measurable; define $q=0$ at the finitely many nodes. This gives a nonnegative measurable representative of the squared derivative error, bounded by the finite cell bounds in step 2.1. The Lebesgue interval-measure and monotonicity facts in [F3] give $\int_K|(u-I_hu)'|^2\le h_K^3\|u''\|_\infty^2$. The open cells are disjoint and their complement consists of finitely many nodes of Lebesgue measure zero. Finite additivity of the measure $E\mapsto\int_Eq$ from [F3], with zero contribution from the nodes where $q=0$, therefore identifies the global Lebesgue squared norm with the sum of these cell integrals. Using $h_K\le h$ and $\sum_Kh_K=1$ gives $\|(u-I_hu)'\|_2^2\le h^2\|u''\|_\infty^2$. Taking nonnegative square roots proves the estimate; endpoint values follow from the nodal definition. [F3, F4, given, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. For every real $v\in H^1_0(0,1)$,

$$\|v\|_{L^2(0,1)}\le\|v'\|_{L^2(0,1)}.$$

Consequently $\|v\|_{H^1(0,1)}\le\sqrt2\,\|v'\|_{L^2(0,1)}$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice and $v$ in the closure of $C_c^\infty(0,1)$ in the $H^1$ norm.

[F1] [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]: for every $\varepsilon>0$, some $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(0,1)$ satisfies $\|v-\varphi\|_{H^1}<\varepsilon$.

[F2] [[thm-ftc-second-part]]: a smooth function's increment is the integral of its derivative.

[F3] [[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]: on an interval of length one, $\int|g|\le\|g\|_{L^2}$.

[F4] [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]: for $k=1,p=2$, $\|v\|_{H^1}^2=\|v\|_2^2+\|v'\|_2^2$.

## Proof

1.1 For $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(0,1)$, [F2] gives $\varphi(x)=\int_0^x\varphi'(t)\,dt$. Hence $|\varphi(x)|\le\int_0^1|\varphi'(t)|\,dt\le\|\varphi'\|_2$ by [F3]; integrating this pointwise bound over an interval of length one yields $\|\varphi\|_2\le\|\varphi'\|_2$. [F2, F3, given]

2.1 Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $\varphi$ by [F1]. The triangle inequality and step 1.1 give $\|v\|_2\le\|\varphi\|_2+\varepsilon\le\|\varphi'\|_2+\varepsilon\le\|v'\|_2+2\varepsilon$. Since this holds for every positive $\varepsilon$, $\|v\|_2\le\|v'\|_2$. By [F4], squaring and adding the derivative norm proves the $H^1$ estimate. [F1, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $V$ be a Hilbert space and let $V_h\subseteq V$ be a subspace. Suppose the exact form $a$ is coercive with constant $\alpha>0$ in the norm $\|\cdot\|_V$. Let $a_h$ be a discrete form on $V_h$ and suppose

$$|a_h(v_h,v_h)-a(v_h,v_h)|\le\eta_h\|v_h\|_V^2\qquad(v_h\in V_h)$$

for some $\eta_h\ge0$. Then $a_h$ is coercive with constant at least $\alpha-\eta_h$ whenever $\eta_h<\alpha$. In particular, if $\eta_h\le\alpha/2$, then its coercivity constant is at least $\alpha/2$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A Hilbert space $V$, a subspace $V_h$, a coercive form $a$ with constant $\alpha>0$, a discrete form $a_h$, and the diagonal defect bound with constant $\eta_h$.

[F1] [[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]: coercivity means $\operatorname{Re}a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2$; symmetry is not required.

[A1] For every $v_h\in V_h$, $|a_h(v_h,v_h)-a(v_h,v_h)|\le\eta_h\|v_h\|_V^2$.

## Proof

1.1 Fix $v_h\in V_h$. By coercivity [F1] and the defect hypothesis [A1], $\operatorname{Re}a_h(v_h,v_h)=\operatorname{Re}a(v_h,v_h)+\operatorname{Re}(a_h(v_h,v_h)-a(v_h,v_h))\ge(\alpha-\eta_h)\|v_h\|_V^2$. [given, F1, A1, algebra]

2.1 If $\eta_h<\alpha$, then $\alpha-\eta_h>0$, so the inequality in step 1.1 is precisely coercivity with that constant. If $\eta_h\le\alpha/2$, then $\alpha-\eta_h\ge\alpha/2$. [step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, $a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ a bounded coercive form with boundedness constant $M$ and coercivity constant $\alpha>0$, and $F:V\to\mathbb K$ a bounded functional linear in the real case and conjugate-linear in the complex test argument. Let $V_h\subseteq V$ be finite-dimensional, and let $a_h:V_h\times V_h\to\mathbb K$ and $F_h:V_h\to\mathbb K$ be bounded, with $F_h$ having the same test-linearity as $F$, and $a_h$ coercive with constant $\alpha_h>0$ in the inherited norm. There are unique exact and discrete solutions $u$ and $u_h$, and

$$\|u-u_h\|_V\le\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\left((1+M/\alpha_h)\|u-v_h\|_V+\frac{\delta_{a,h}(v_h)+\delta_{F,h}}{\alpha_h}\right),$$

where the defects are those of [[def-variational-crime-error-framework]]. For a family of meshes this is a uniform estimate whenever $\inf_h\alpha_h>0$ and the displayed approximation and defect terms are uniformly controlled. The term $\delta_{F,h}$ retains source approximation and data oscillation.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; $V,a,F,V_h,a_h,F_h$ with the Hilbert, boundedness, coercivity, and finite-dimensional hypotheses of the Statement.

[F1] [[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]: $|a(v,w)|\le M\|v\|_V\|w\|_V$ and $\operatorname{Re}a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2$; the real bilinear case does not require symmetry.

[F2] [[thm-lax-milgram]] under [[def-countable-choice]]: a bounded coercive form on a Hilbert space with a bounded functional has a unique solution to its variational equation.

[F3] [[cor-finite-dimensional-subspaces-are-closed]]: a finite-dimensional subspace of a normed space is closed; therefore $V_h$ with the inherited inner product is a Hilbert space.

[F4] [[def-variational-crime-error-framework]]: $\delta_{a,h}(v_h)$ and $\delta_{F,h}$ are the indicated suprema of the form and load defects against nonzero tests in $V_h$.

[A1] $a_h$ is bounded and $\operatorname{Re}a_h(v_h,v_h)\ge\alpha_h\|v_h\|_V^2$ on $V_h$; $F_h$ is bounded.

## Proof

1.1 The hypotheses on $V,a,F$ are exactly those of [F2], so [F2] gives a unique $u\in V$ satisfying $a(u,v)=F(v)$ for every $v\in V$. [F1, F2, given]

1.2 By [F3], $V_h$ is closed in $V$, hence complete in its inherited Hilbert norm. The restriction of $a_h$ is bounded and coercive by [A1], and $F_h$ is bounded; applying [F2] on $V_h$ gives a unique $u_h\in V_h$ with $a_h(u_h,w_h)=F_h(w_h)$ for every $w_h\in V_h$. [F2, F3, A1, given]

2.1 Fix any $v_h\in V_h$ and put $e_h:=u_h-v_h$. Discrete coercivity and the discrete equation give $\alpha_h\|e_h\|_V^2\le\operatorname{Re}a_h(e_h,e_h)=\operatorname{Re}(F_h(e_h)-a_h(v_h,e_h))$. [A1, step 1.2, choose]

3.1 Since $e_h\in V_h\subseteq V$, the exact equation gives $F(e_h)=a(u,e_h)$, and $F_h(e_h)-a_h(v_h,e_h)=[F_h(e_h)-F(e_h)]+a(u-v_h,e_h)+[a(v_h,e_h)-a_h(v_h,e_h)]$. The boundedness of $a$ [F1] and the defect definitions [F4] therefore imply $\alpha_h\|e_h\|_V^2\le\left(\delta_{F,h}+M\|u-v_h\|_V+\delta_{a,h}(v_h)\right)\|e_h\|_V$. [F1, F4, given, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 If $e_h=0$ the comparison is immediate; otherwise divide step 3.1 by $\alpha_h\|e_h\|_V$ and use $\|u-u_h\|_V\le\|u-v_h\|_V+\|e_h\|_V$. This proves the displayed bound for each $v_h$, and taking the infimum proves the theorem. [step 3.1, algebra] ∎

      url: https://jschoeberl.github.io/iFEM/FEM/nonconforming.html
---

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, $a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ bounded and coercive, and $F$ a bounded functional with the test-linearity required by $a$. Let $V_h$ be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space with norm $\|\cdot\|_h$, not necessarily a subspace of $V$. Suppose the algebraic sum $X_h=V+V_h$ is equipped with a norm extending these norms, and $\widetilde a_h:X_h\times V_h\to\mathbb K$ is a bounded extension of a discrete form $a_h$ with bound $M_h$. Assume $a_h$ is coercive on $V_h$ with constant $\alpha_h>0$, and let $F_h$ be bounded on $V_h$ with the matching test-linearity. The exact and discrete equations have unique solutions $u$ and $u_h$, and

$$\|u-u_h\|_h\le(1+M_h/\alpha_h)\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_h+\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)/\alpha_h,$$

where $\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)=\sup_{w_h\ne0}|F_h(w_h)-\widetilde a_h(u,w_h)|/\|w_h\|_h$. The estimate requires the bounded extension and does not assert that every nonconforming, penalty, or discontinuous Galerkin form has one.

For a family of these problems, suppose $M_h\le\overline M<\infty$ and $\alpha_h\ge\underline\alpha>0$ uniformly. Writing $E_h=\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_h$, the uniform bound is
$$\|u-u_h\|_h\le(1+\overline M/\underline\alpha)E_h+\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)/\underline\alpha.$$
Thus uniform control of $E_h$ and $\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)$ gives a uniform error budget; if both tend to zero, the errors tend to zero, and if both are $O(h^p)$ for a fixed $p>0$, the error is $O(h^p)$. No rate is inferred without those approximation, residual, and stability bounds.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; the exact Hilbert problem on $V$; the nonconforming space $V_h$ and common comparison norm on $X_h$; a bounded extension $\widetilde a_h$; discrete coercivity $\alpha_h>0$; and a bounded discrete load.

[F1] [[thm-lax-milgram]] under [[def-countable-choice]]: the exact bounded coercive Hilbert problem has a unique solution.

[F2] By definition, $\widetilde a_h$ agrees with $a_h$ on $V_h\times V_h$ and $|\widetilde a_h(z,w_h)|\le M_h\|z\|_h\|w_h\|_h$ on $X_h\times V_h$ ([[def-variational-crime-error-framework]]).

[A1] $\operatorname{Re}a_h(v_h,v_h)\ge\alpha_h\|v_h\|_h^2$ for every $v_h\in V_h$.

[A2] $\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)$ is the consistency residual at the exact solution, as defined in [[def-variational-crime-error-framework]].

## Proof

1.1 Apply [F1] on $V$ to obtain the unique exact solution $u$. [F1, given]

1.2 The finite-dimensional Hilbert problem on $V_h$ has bounded coercive form $a_h$ and bounded load $F_h$, so the same Lax–Milgram theorem [F1] gives a unique $u_h\in V_h$. [F1, A1, given]

2.1 Fix $v_h\in V_h$ and set $e_h:=u_h-v_h$. Then $e_h\in V_h$, and [A1] gives $\alpha_h\|e_h\|_h^2\le\operatorname{Re}a_h(e_h,e_h)=\operatorname{Re}(F_h(e_h)-\widetilde a_h(v_h,e_h))$. [A1, step 1.2, choose]

3.1 By the discrete equation and extension identity, $a_h(e_h,e_h)=\widetilde a_h(u-v_h,e_h)+F_h(e_h)-\widetilde a_h(u,e_h)$. The extension bound [F2] and residual definition [A2] therefore give $\alpha_h\|e_h\|_h^2\le(M_h\|u-v_h\|_h+\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u))\|e_h\|_h$. [F2, A1, A2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 If $e_h=0$ there is nothing to divide by; otherwise divide step 3.1 by $\alpha_h\|e_h\|_h$. The triangle inequality gives $\|u-u_h\|_h\le(1+M_h/\alpha_h)\|u-v_h\|_h+\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)/\alpha_h$. Taking the infimum over $v_h$ proves the per-mesh bound. For the stated family, replace $M_h/\alpha_h$ by $\overline M/\underline\alpha$ and $1/\alpha_h$ by $1/\underline\alpha$. The resulting constants are independent of $h$, yielding the stated uniform, convergence and rate consequences when the two explicit error terms have the corresponding control. [step 3.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the geometry setting of [[def-geometry-lift-and-tensor-discrepancy]], and suppose $\Omega_h$ has a nonempty finite measurable partition into bounded cells $\{K\}$, with $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and $h:=\max_Kh_K$. For real-valued $U,W\in C^1(\Omega)$ with $\nabla U,\nabla W\in L^2(\Omega)$, put $v:=U\circ\Phi_h$ and $w:=W\circ\Phi_h$, and assume their gradients are square-integrable on each cell. Then the physical exact form $a(U,W)$ pulled back by $\Phi_h$ is $a_h^{\mathrm{lift}}(v,w)$. Suppose the implemented tensors $\widetilde B_h$ are real symmetric and measurable, with $\eta_{G,K}<\infty$. The form $\widetilde a_h(v,w):=\sum_K\int_K\nabla v^T\widetilde B_h\nabla w$ satisfies

$$|a_h^{\mathrm{lift}}(v,w)-\widetilde a_h(v,w)|\le\sum_K\eta_{G,K}\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(K)}\|\nabla w\|_{L^2(K)}\le\eta_G\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\Omega_h)}\|\nabla w\|_{L^2(\Omega_h)},$$

where $\eta_G:=\max_K\eta_{G,K}$. If $\eta_{G,K}\le C_Gh_K^s$ for $s>0$, the form defect is at most $C_Gh^s\|\nabla v\|_2\|\nabla w\|_2$. Moreover, if $J_h\ge j_->0$, $0<L$, and $\|D\Phi_h\|_{L^\infty,\mathrm{op}}\le L$, then $B_h\succeq\beta I$ with $\beta=j_-\lambda/L^2$. For the stability conclusion, let $Z_h$ be a real Hilbert space of pullback functions with inner product $\int_{\Omega_h}\nabla v\cdot\nabla w$, so its norm is $\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\Omega_h)}$. Restrict the exact and implemented forms to $Z_h$. If $\eta_G\le\beta/2$, the implemented form is coercive on $Z_h$ with constant at least $\beta/2$. The rate assumption is separate from the lift; neither it nor completeness of the gradient-norm space follows from a lift alone.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; the geometry definition; a nonempty finite measurable cell partition; physical functions $U,W$ and their pullbacks $v,w$ as stated; a real symmetric measurable tensor $A$ with $\lambda I\preceq A\preceq\Lambda I$; a $C^1$ diffeomorphism with positive Jacobian; measurable symmetric implemented tensors $\widetilde B_h$ with finite cell discrepancies; and, for the coercivity conclusion, the real Hilbert space $Z_h$ with the gradient inner product specified in the Statement.

## Statement

Let $0=x_0<\cdots<x_N=1$ be a finite partition with cell lengths $h_K$ and maximum $h$. Let $A\in C^2([0,1])$, and let $v_h,w_h$ be continuous piecewise-linear functions. Define the exact and midpoint stiffness forms by

$$a(v_h,w_h):=\sum_K\int_KA(x)v_h'(x)w_h'(x)\,dx,\qquad a_h(v_h,w_h):=\sum_Kh_KA(m_K)v_h'|_Kw_h'|_K,$$

where $m_K$ is the cell midpoint and the cell derivatives are constant. Then

$$|a(v_h,w_h)-a_h(v_h,w_h)|\le\frac{h^2}{24}\|A''\|_{L^\infty(0,1)}\|v_h'\|_{L^2(0,1)}\|w_h'\|_{L^2(0,1)}.$$

The midpoint rule is exact for this stiffness integrand when $A$ is affine; for a general $C^2$ coefficient the displayed defect is retained. The bound is exact-arithmetic quadrature error, separate from roundoff.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite partition, $A\in C^2([0,1])$, and continuous piecewise-linear $v_h,w_h$.

[F1] [[alg-composite-midpoint-rule]]: on one cell $K$, the midpoint value times $h_K$ is the one-panel midpoint quadrature rule.

[F2] [[thm-composite-midpoint-error-bound]]: for $g\in C^2(K)$, the one-panel error is at most $h_K^3\|g''\|_{L^\infty(K)}/24$.

[F3] [[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]]: the integral over $[0,1]$ is the sum of cell integrals.

[F4] [[lem-triangle-inequality-finite]]: the absolute value of the sum of cell errors is bounded by their absolute values' sum.

[F5] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: the sum of products of two finite real lists is bounded by the product of their Euclidean norms.

[F6] [[thm-extreme-value-r]]: the continuous function $|A''|$ has a finite maximum on $[0,1]$.

## Proof

1.1 On a cell $K$, $v_h'|_K$ and $w_h'|_K$ are constants, so $g_K(x):=A(x)v_h'|_Kw_h'|_K$ is $C^2$; the discrete sample is the one-panel midpoint rule [F1]. Also $\|g_K''\|_\infty\le\|A''\|_\infty|v_h'|_K|w_h'|_K$. Applying [F2] with $n=1$ bounds the cell error by $h_K^3\|A''\|_\infty|v_h'|_K|w_h'|_K/24$. [given, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 Since $\|v_h'\|_{L^2(K)}=\sqrt{h_K}|v_h'|_K$ and similarly for $w_h$, step 1.1 equals at most $h_K^2\|A''\|_\infty\|v_h'\|_{L^2(K)}\|w_h'\|_{L^2(K)}/24$. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Repeated application of [F3], by induction over the finite partition, expresses the total form difference as the sum of cell errors. Then [F4] and step 2.1 bound its absolute value by $h^2\|A''\|_\infty/24$ times $\sum_K\|v_h'\|_{L^2(K)}\|w_h'\|_{L^2(K)}$. Apply [F5] to these finite cell-norm lists; the result is the displayed global estimate. [F3, F4, F5, F6, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Put $V:=H^1_0(0,1)$ with its $H^1$ norm, and let $V_h\subseteq V$ be a finite-dimensional conforming piecewise-linear space on an interval partition with maximum cell width $h$. Define $a(v,w)=\int_0^1A v'w'$ and let $a_h$ use one midpoint quadrature sample per cell. Let $F$ and $F_h$ be bounded exact and discrete loads, and put $\delta_{F,h}:=\sup_{w_h\ne0}|F(w_h)-F_h(w_h)|/\|w_h\|_{H^1}$. Then the exact and discrete solutions satisfy

$$\|u-u_h\|_{H^1}\le(1+2M/\alpha)\sqrt2h\|u''\|_\infty+\frac2\alpha\left(\frac{C_Ah^2}{24}(\|u'\|_2+h\|u''\|_\infty)+\delta_{F,h}\right).$$

The explicit $\delta_{F,h}$ is the data/source oscillation term; no rate or vanishing of it is asserted without an additional load approximation hypothesis. Here coercivity follows directly because every sampled coefficient satisfies $A(m_K)\ge\alpha$; this special argument does not infer stability from quadrature exactness.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; $V=H^1_0(0,1)$; a conforming finite-dimensional P1 space $V_h$; $u\in C^2\cap V$ with $I_hu\in V_h$; $A\in C^2$ with $\alpha\le A\le M$; and bounded loads $F,F_h$.

[F1] [[lem-w-one-two-is-a-hilbert-space]] and [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]: under Countable Choice, $H^1_0(0,1)$ is a Hilbert space for its $H^1$ inner product.

[F2] [[lem-one-dimensional-zero-boundary-poincare]]: $\|v\|_2\le\|v'\|_2$ for $v\in H^1_0(0,1)$.

[F3] [[lem-one-dimensional-p1-interpolation-error]]: $\|(u-I_hu)'\|_2\le h\|u''\|_\infty$.

[F4] [[lem-midpoint-quadrature-defect-for-p1-stiffness]]: $|a(v_h,w_h)-a_h(v_h,w_h)|\le C_Ah^2\|v_h'\|_2\|w_h'\|_2/24$.

[F5] [[thm-first-strang-lemma-for-conforming-perturbed-galerkin]]: error is bounded by best approximation plus the form and load defects divided by discrete coercivity.

[A1] The exact and discrete equations are $a(u,v)=F(v)$ and $a_h(u_h,w_h)=F_h(w_h)$, and $\delta_{F,h}$ is as in the Statement.

## Proof

1.1 By [F2], $\|v\|_{H^1}^2=\|v\|_2^2+\|v'\|_2^2\le2\|v'\|_2^2$. Hence $a$ is bounded by $M$ in the $H^1$ norm and coercive with constant $\alpha/2$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

1.2 On each cell $K$, $A(m_K)\ge\alpha$, so $a_h(v_h,v_h)=\sum_Kh_KA(m_K)|v_h'|_K^2\ge\alpha\|v_h'\|_2^2$. By [F2], $\|v_h\|_{H^1}^2\le2\|v_h'\|_2^2$, hence $a_h(v_h,v_h)\ge(\alpha/2)\|v_h\|_{H^1}^2$ and $\alpha_h\ge\alpha/2$. [F2, given, algebra]

1.3 By [F3] and [F2], $\|u-I_hu\|_{H^1}\le\sqrt2\|(u-I_hu)'\|_2\le\sqrt2h\|u''\|_\infty$. Also the triangle inequality gives $\|(I_hu)'\|_2\le\|u'\|_2+h\|u''\|_\infty$. [F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F5] with comparison function $I_hu$. Its best-approximation term is bounded by step 1.3; [F4] bounds its form defect by $C_Ah^2(\|u'\|_2+h\|u''\|_\infty)/24$ because $\|w_h'\|_2\le\|w_h\|_{H^1}$. The load defect is exactly $\delta_{F,h}$ by [A1]. [F4, F5, A1, step 1.3]

3.1 Substitute $M$ from step 1.1 and $\alpha_h\ge\alpha/2$ from step 1.2 into the first-Strang bound in step 2.1. This gives the displayed estimate and retains the full load defect. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Its unique perturbed solution $\widetilde u_h$ satisfies

$$\|u-\widetilde u_h\|_a\le\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_a+\frac{\sqrt M}{\alpha_h}\rho_h,$$

where $\rho_h:=\sup_{w_h\ne0}|F_h(w_h)-a_h(u_h^G,w_h)|/\|w_h\|_V$, defined as zero if $V_h=\{0\}$. This uses the exact Galerkin solution as a baseline; $\rho_h$ must be bounded from the actual form and load defects.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Countable-Choice bounded coercive Hermitian Galerkin setting, its exact Galerkin solution $u_h^G$, and a bounded coercive perturbed form/load with the stated residual $\rho_h$, including its zero-space convention.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and let $d\in\{2,3\}$. Let $\mathcal T_h$ be a matching shape-regular affine simplicial mesh as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. Let $V_h$ be a conforming zero-boundary P1 Lagrange subspace of a Hilbert space $V$, with $V_h\subseteq V$, and let $I_hu\in V_h$ be the global nodal interpolant of $u\in H^2(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$ whose boundary nodal values vanish. Then a constant $C_I$ depending only on the reference P1 element and shape-regularity bound satisfies

$$\|u-u_h\|_V\le(1+M/\alpha_h)C_VC_Ih|u|_{H^2(\Omega)}+\frac{\delta_{a,h}(I_hu)+\delta_{F,h}}{\alpha_h}.$$

If $\alpha_h\ge\alpha_*>0$ uniformly, the displayed approximation contribution is $O(h)$; the geometry, quadrature, and load defects remain separate terms and require their own estimates.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; $d=2$ or $3$; a matching shape-regular affine simplicial mesh; a conforming P1 Lagrange family in $V$; $u\in H^2\cap C(\overline\Omega)$ with zero boundary nodal values; a global interpolant $I_hu\in V_h$; and the bounded/coercive exact and discrete forms and loads of the first Strang theorem.

[F2] [[def-reference-finite-element-and-unisolvent-dofs]]: an unisolvent reference element defines its interpolation operator from its degrees of freedom.

[F3] [[def-broken-and-conforming-polynomial-spaces]]: conformity means matching polynomial traces on each interior facet, and the zero-boundary subspace has zero polynomial trace on every boundary facet.

[F4] [[thm-local-finite-element-interpolation-estimates]]: for the P1 Lagrange element, $p=2$, $\ell=r=2$, $m=1$, and $\ell>d/p$, $|u-I_Ku|_{H^1(K)}\le C h_K|u|_{H^2(K)}$ uniformly on the shape-regular affine mesh.

[F5] [[thm-first-strang-lemma-for-conforming-perturbed-galerkin]]: the conforming error is bounded by its best-approximation term and the actual discrete form/load defects.

[A1] The global nodal interpolant has matching traces and zero boundary nodal values, and it belongs to $V_h\subseteq V$ as stipulated in the Statement.

[A2] The reference P1 nodal functionals are bounded on $W^{2,2}$, as assumed in the Statement; no point-evaluation theorem or stronger choice principle is used to infer this hypothesis here.

1.2 On a shared facet, both neighboring P1 traces are affine and have the same values at every facet vertex, so the traces agree. Identify each such function with its two cellwise slopes, a two-dimensional space $V_h$ of piecewise-constant fields. For $\omega_h=s_L\mathbf1_{[0,1/2]}+s_R\mathbf1_{(1/2,1]}$, define its associated broken function by $U_{\omega_h}(x)=s_Lx$ on the left cell and $U_{\omega_h}(x)=s_R(x-1)$ on the right cell. The left basis function $\phi_L(x)=2x$ on the first cell and $0$ on the second corresponds to slope field $\omega_L=2\mathbf1_{[0,1/2]}$; it has residual $F_h(\omega_L)-\widetilde a_h(g_u,\omega_L)=-1/4$. ## Example

For Lebesgue measure on $[-1,1]$, the two-node Gaussian rule has nodes $\pm1/\sqrt3$ and weights $1$. The supplier theorem gives exactness through degree three, but the error on $x^4$ is $8/45$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $a=-1$, $b=1$, $m=2$, $r=3=2m-1$, and Lebesgue measure $\mu$ on $[-1,1]$.

[F2] [[thm-monic-gauss-orthogonal-polynomials-exist-uniquely]]: the monic degree-two polynomial $p_2$ is orthogonal to every polynomial of degree below two.

[F4] [[thm-gauss-rule-exact-through-degree-2m-minus-1-and-positive-weights]]: the rule integrates every polynomial of degree at most $2m-1$ exactly.

[F5] [[thm-ftc-second-part]]: the integral of a continuous derivative on $[-1,1]$ is the primitive's endpoint difference.

## Definition

Use the smooth nonlinear program convention of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]]: minimize a $C^2$
objective $f:U\to\mathbb R$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, subject to
$h(x)=0$ and componentwise $g(x)\le0$. Fix a current point $x\in U$ and a
symmetric positive-definite matrix $B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$. The
**SQP quadratic subproblem** is
$$\min_{p\in\mathbb R^n}\quad \nabla f(x)^Tp+\tfrac12p^TBp \quad\text{subject to}\quad h(x)+Dh(x)p=0,\quad g(x)+Dg(x)p\le0.$$
The variable $p$ is the proposed displacement. Its feasible set is the
polyhedron defined by the displayed affine constraints. A constraint index
$i$ is **active at $p$** when $g_i(x)+Dg_i(x)p=0$. For equality multiplier
$\nu$ and inequality multipliers $\lambda\ge0$, a **KKT tuple** for the
subproblem satisfies primal feasibility,
$$Bp+\nabla f(x)+Dh(x)^T\nu+Dg(x)^T\lambda=0, \qquad \lambda_i\bigl(g_i(x)+Dg_i(x)p\bigr)=0\quad(1\le i\le m).$$
Rows of $Dh(x)$ and active rows of $Dg(x)$ are stacked in that order in the
subproblem KKT matrix $\begin{bmatrix}B&A^T\\A&0\end{bmatrix}$.

All inequality signs and multiplier signs here agree with the source program:
$g_i\le0$ and $\lambda_i\ge0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A $C^2$ program, a current point $x$, and a symmetric positive-
definite model matrix $B$.

[F1] [[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]] fixes the
program's equality and componentwise $g_i\le0$ inequality convention, with
Lagrangian $f+\nu^Th+\lambda^Tg$ and $\lambda\ge0$.

[A1] The model matrix $B$ is symmetric positive definite.

## Proof

1.1 Differentiability at $x$ gives the affine first-order models $h(x)+Dh(x)p$ and $g(x)+Dg(x)p$; the positive-definite quadratic model is finite for every $p\in\mathbb R^n$. Thus the displayed feasible set is a well-defined polyhedron, possibly empty. [given, A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 For an active affine inequality, the multiplier convention in the Lagrangian contributes $Dg_i(x)^T\lambda_i$ to stationarity, while complementarity is $\lambda_i(g_i(x)+Dg_i(x)p)=0$. Hence the stated KKT tuple uses the same sign convention as [F1]. [F1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Use the smooth program, dimensions, gradient conventions, and Lagrangian
$L(x,\nu,\lambda)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\lambda^Tg(x)$ of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]]. Let $\rho>0$,
$\nu\in\mathbb R^p$, and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m_+$. The equality
augmented Lagrangian is
$$\mathcal L^E_\rho(x,\nu)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\tfrac{\rho}{2}\|h(x)\|_2^2.$$
For inequalities, with $[z]_i^+=\max\{z_i,0\}$, the projected
(Powell–Hestenes–Rockafellar) augmented Lagrangian is
$$\mathcal L_\rho(x,\nu,\lambda)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\tfrac{\rho}{2}\|h(x)\|_2^2+ \frac{\|[\lambda+\rho g(x)]_+\|_2^2-\|\lambda\|_2^2}{2\rho}.$$
After an inner candidate $x^+$ is produced, the multiplier update is
$$\nu^+=\nu+\rho h(x^+),\qquad \lambda^+=[\lambda+\rho g(x^+)]_+.$$
The bracket is componentwise. A **declared inner stationarity residual** is
$\|\nabla_x\mathcal L_\rho(x^+,\nu,\lambda)\|_2$; an inner procedure must
report the residual it achieved or an explicit failure status.

The equality and inequality formulas are distinct branches. For an inequality
with $\lambda_i+\rho g_i(x)>0$, its summand equals
$\lambda_i g_i(x)+\rho g_i(x)^2/2$; when
$\lambda_i+\rho g_i(x)\le0$, its summand is constant in $x$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The smooth program, $\rho>0$, equality multiplier $\nu$, and
componentwise nonnegative inequality multiplier $\lambda$.

[F1] [[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]] uses $g_i\le0$
and the Lagrangian $f+\nu^Th+\lambda^Tg$.

[A1] The penalty parameter satisfies $\rho>0$ and the inequality
multiplier satisfies $\lambda\ge0$.

## Proof

1.1 For any scalar $s=\lambda_i+\rho g_i(x)$, the identity $([s]_+)^2-\lambda_i^2=(s^2-\lambda_i^2)$ when $s>0$ expands to $2\rho\lambda_i g_i+\rho^2g_i^2$; when $s\le0$, $[s]_+=0$. This gives the two stated inequality branches and shows they agree in value at their boundary. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Differentiating the equality branch gives multiplier update $\nu+\rho h(x)$. On the positive inequality branch, differentiating its summand gives $[\lambda_i+\rho g_i(x)]_+Dg_i(x)^T$; on the nonpositive branch it gives zero. Thus the projected update is nonnegative and is consistent with the displayed piecewise gradient. [given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}$ have full row rank, where $0\le r\le n$,
and let $H\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric and positive definite on
$\ker A$: $z^THz>0$ whenever $0\ne z\in\ker A$. Then
$$K=\begin{bmatrix}H&A^T\\A&0\end{bmatrix}$$
is nonsingular. Here the zero-row case $r=0$ is allowed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The matrix hypotheses in the Statement and the SQP KKT block
convention of [[def-sqp-linearized-quadratic-subproblem]].

[A1] $A$ has full row rank, and $H$ is positive definite on $\ker A$, as
stated.

[F1] [[def-sqp-linearized-quadratic-subproblem]] stacks the equality rows and
independent active inequality rows into $A$ and uses the displayed saddle
matrix.

## Proof

1.1 Suppose $K\binom{z}{\mu}=0$. Its lower block gives $Az=0$, so $z\in\ker A$; multiplying the upper block $Hz+A^T\mu=0$ by $z^T$ gives $z^THz=0$. Positive definiteness on $\ker A$ forces $z=0$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 With $z=0$, the upper block gives $A^T\mu=0$. Full row rank of $A$ means $A^T$ is injective, so $\mu=0$. Thus the square matrix $K$ has trivial kernel and is nonsingular; when $r=0$, the same argument says $H$ has trivial kernel. [given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

      locator: "Chapter 18 §18.5, L1 merit and directional decrease, printed pp. 542–545 / PDF pp. 560–563."
